items.title: Rizeigat clan bids for Hemedti’s ear, Burhan’s US visa troubles, Kordofan battles come to head as RSF presses ahead in Blue Nile, Kiir re-engineers electoral scene
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . As world leaders gathered in New York this week for talks at the United Nations General Assembly, Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan had to watch the proceeding from afar. And that is because, while the military leader had been penciled in to give a speech to the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, the US denied his visa. For Sudanese officials familiar with the internal planning, the move doesn’t come as a complete surprise, given that the US had sanctioned Burhan last year and the relationship has become increasingly fractious. But the visa denial is yet another sign of the frustration and polarization that dominates talks over a humanitarian truce, ceasefire and political settlement to Sudan’s war. Sources in New York and others familiar with communications between Sudan, regional capitals and the US described efforts to mitigate the crisis, which they viewed as US pressure on Sudan to accept a 90-day humanitarian truce, while emphasizing that the government would not back down from its core position. But the military wasn’t the only one facing a political crisis this week. In Darfur, the Nawaiba, one of the Rizeigat’s main clans in East Darfur, announced it was withdrawing from the nazirate of Musa Madibo, the head of the Rizeigat. The Nawaib were keen to underline they still support the RSF leadership, who hail from the Rizeigat. According to a Rizeigat tribal leader informed of discussions within several of the tribe’s components, the move is really a bid to open a direct line of communication with RSF Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo. Nonetheless, for the RSF, which has already seen internecine fighting among its base, with loyalists jockeying for rungs in the broader hierarchy, the move’s catalytic effect could create an even larger opening for rival military and political actors to exploit the crisis. Away from political management, Sudan’s two main battlefronts continue to churn. Following weeks of military gains in North Kordofan, fighting is narrowing in on the remaining RSF-held positions. Both sides are upping the ante with front line deployments to try to sway the fight for the state one way or another. The military holds a much less firm position in the Blue Nile, even as it continues to prevent being overrun. With its eyes set on the state’s capital of Damazin, the RSF unsuccessfully attempted to take key towns that would have allowed it to create linkages in its supply chain between its positions on the southeastern border with Ethiopia and its forces farther south near South Sudan. As wars engulf its neighbors, South Sudan seems set for its own breaking point. In a continuation of his efforts to marginalize his one-time enemy, one-time co-leader in power former Vice President Riek Machar, Kiir overhauled the country’s electoral process this week, appointing a new elections commission chair, amending the electoral law and dissolving the transitional government. An opposition source called the move politically biased, saying electoral rules set specific grounds for removing the chair, including proven bias, inability to perform the job or serious misconduct. Elections are set to be held in December, and while voices in South Sudan and beyond continue to warn that current government practices are widening divides, Kiir continues to press ahead, pushing the country, perhaps, to be yet another blazing front in a region on fire. *** Rizeigat clan exits Madibo’s nazirate in bid for direct line to Hemedti, source says Still from the Nawaiba clan’s video statement recorded in East Darfur’s Firdos locality, September 13. Photo: Abdelmged Abdelhmeed via Facebook. After months of disagreements over leadership and representation within one of Darfur’s largest and most influential Arab tribes, the Nawaiba, one of the Rizeigat’s main clans in East Darfur, announced last week that it was withdrawing from the nazirate of Musa Madibo, the head of the Rizeigat. “We made numerous concessions throughout history under the nazirate administration, most recently under [Madibo],” Omar Nour, the head of the Nawaiba administration’s executive office, said in a video statement made on September 13 while surrounded by Nawaiba omdas. “However, these concessions were misinterpreted, and the reward was blatant and continuous injustice and inequality among the Rizeigat factions by the [Madibo] administration and his deputy.” Nour said that the 24 Nawaiba omdas have withdrawn from “all committees and bodies” formed by the nazir and are no longer subordinate to him. Nevertheless, they pledged continued support for RSF Commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo and said the Nawaiba would remain bound by the directives of East Darfur’s RSF-affiliated state security committee and the Firdos locality security committee, where the group has its main social base. The group would continue coordinating with the committees on security and stability in its areas, he said. Nour told Mada Masr that the decision was part of an effort to reorganize the group’s tribal affairs and clarify which authority it answers to, and not a break with the tribe’s components. Yet beyond a Madibo-Nawaiba matter is a broader shift in how some parts of the tribe want to deal with the RSF leadership, a Rizeigat tribal leader informed of discussions within several of the tribe’s components told Mada Masr. For the Nawaiba, that means establishing a direct channel to Hemedti rather than relying on the nazirate to represent them — a prospect the RSF commander has to approach with caution to avoid unsettling the wider relationship with his group’s main social base. The Madibo family has dominated the Rizeigat nazirate in Darfur for decades. Musa Madibo, the current nazir, is aligned with the RSF, whose fighters are drawn largely from the Rizeigat and whose ranks include many commanders from the tribe. The Nawaiba’s decision to withdraw from the nazirate followed internal discussions and consultations that had been underway within the clan for at least five months, a tribal administration source in Firdos and a Nawaiba omda told Mada Masr. The dispute is rooted in accumulated grievances over how the nazirate manages the tribe’s affairs and how its different components are represented within it, amid a growing sense within the Nawaiba leadership of unequal treatment, the omda and a source close to the Nawaiba administration said. The Nawaiba, the omda said, had been “wronged in obtaining their rights within the nazirate.” Two sources close to Madibo said the nazir considers the Nawaiba “family” and is prepared to sit down with them to address the issues behind the withdrawal. The tribal leadership does not regard the move as a rupture with the Nawaiba, one of the sources told Mada Masr, but as a dispute that can be contained through dialogue, particularly given the sensitivity of it spreading to other Rizeigat components. But for the Rizeigat leader informed of the discussions, the dispute is fundamentally an attempt to bypass traditional channels of tribal representation and negotiation altogether rather than being a Madibo-Nawaiba administrative disagreement. Some Rizeigat components have been discussing the losses and strains their communities continue to face during the war, including displacement and insecurity, recruitment and the presence of armed forces in their areas and families dealing with sons who have been killed, captured or have gone missing, the leader said. At the same time, the RSF’s control of Darfur has changed the distribution of power across the region. This has left some constituencies questioning how their relationship with the RSF is being managed and whether their tribal leaders can still effectively represent their interests, including their place in the power structure, to the group’s leadership, the leader said. Under this pressure from their communities, the Nawaiba leaders want a direct channel to Hemedti through which they can raise their concerns themselves, he added. The RSF leadership will have to handle this carefully, the leader said. Under the current circumstances, Hemedti cannot confront the Nawaiba directly or treat their position as a rebellion without risking a wider dispute within the Rizeigat, a social base that has remained critical to the RSF since its formation. A confrontation with a major Rizeigat component could carry greater political and social costs for the RSF leadership than any gains it might produce, he said. That makes the Nawaiba dispute part of a broader change in how Hemedti may have to deal with Rizeigat communities in the future. Rather than relying entirely on the nazir or the traditional hierarchy of tribal leadership, he may have to communicate directly with a network of components and competing interests, the leader said. For Madibo, the concern now is not whether the Nawaiba will return to his administration, but whether the nazirate will remain able to monopolize representation of the Rizeigat in dealings with the RSF leadership, according to the leader. The Nawaiba’s move opens the door for other components to do the same. After years of war, the costs of fighting have made social loyalty less available as a “blank check,” he said. That does not mean that the Nawaiba or other components would become independent of the RSF. Rather, their relationship with the group would become more negotiated, he added. “Communities that have paid the price of the war are beginning to say that they have a right to determine what the relationship will look like afterward.” They can use their ability to mobilize men, halt recruitment, influence the movement of civilians and fighters or redefine their relationship with tribal leaders as bargaining tools in their dealings with the RSF leadership, he said. In that sense, the Nawaiba’s decision to leave the nazirate while reaffirming their Rizeigat identity is significant because it allows the group to change its relationship with the tribal leadership without giving up its place within the Rizeigat, according to the leader. The group wants to maintain the channels it relies on to manage security and other consequences of the war in its areas, the leader, a tribal administration source in East Darfur and a government source in the state said. That is why, according to the government source, the Nawaiba took care to define its security and administrative relationship with the RSF institutions in its statement last week. Although the Nawaiba have, for now, explicitly reaffirmed their allegiance to the RSF, a second source from the Rizeigat council said there remains concern that the move’s catalytic effect could create an opening for rival military and political actors to exploit the crisis. *** Military, RSF reinforce positions in North Kordofan With most of North Kordofan now under military control and the battle narrowing around the remaining RSF-held areas, both sides sent new forces to their frontline positions this week ahead of an expected push to settle control over the state. On Sunday, the RSF deployed more than 50 combat vehicles to Mazroub, while additional forces arrived on the western outskirts of Sodary, a military source told Mada Masr. Other RSF units gathered that day in Abu Zaeima, Um Bader and Hamra al-Sheikh in northwestern North Kordofan. The source said the group was seeking to halt the military’s advance by all means, fearing that fighting could once again spread more into Darfur. The military seized most of the state between July and September in two large-scale surprise operations. It is now reinforcing those gains. Thousands of military and allied troops arrived at frontlines in North Kordofan from Khartoum on Tuesday, a second military source told Mada Masr. Their role, the source said, would be to secure territory recently captured by the military, leaving the main attacking forces free to push toward the remaining RSF positions. Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the military’s Special Operations Forces in West Kordofan, told the press on Tuesday that the military is “meters away” from Sodary. The operational objective, he added, was to take full control of North Kordofan and secure it ahead of an advance toward West Kordofan. Didan said RSF deputy commander Abdel Rahim Dagalo arrived in Kordofan from Nyala to reinforce his forces. For the military, Sodary, a link between the Kordofan fronts and the Darfur desert, is strategic because taking the town would effectively bring Mazroub and the remaining RSF-held areas of North Kordofan under military control, a former military officer told Mada Masr. It would also put towns in northern West Kordofan under pressure and open a route toward Darfur, he said. The International Organization for Migration said 3,650 people were displaced from the Um Bader area of Sodary between September 20 and 22 as insecurity worsened. The displaced fled to Sheikan in North Kordofan and to Omdurman in Khartoum, the agency said. *** RSF launches simultaneous drone attacks in North Kordofan, River Nile Two people were killed and 20 were wounded when RSF suicide drones struck neighborhoods in Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, the Sudan Doctors Network said on Sunday. An official in North Kordofan told Mada Masr that more than 11 RSF drones attacked the city from early morning until midday. The military’s ground-based air defenses intercepted some of them before they reached their targets, the official said. He described the attacks as an attempt by the RSF to make up for recent territorial losses in North Kordofan and to respond to the military’s expanding operations against the group. The strikes also destroyed two warehouses holding hundreds of thousands of schoolbooks and other educational materials, the United Nations Children’s Fund said. The supplies had been intended for distribution to children in West Bara, Bara and Um Dam Haj Ahmed starting October, when the new school year is due to start. Angela Kearney, UNICEF’s representative in Sudan, said the destruction was a setback for children as efforts were underway to return them to school after many had already lost years of education because of the war. On the same day, another drone targeted the Kokiti area west of Bara, but the military’s air defenses shot it down, according to the military. RSF drones also reached northeastern Sudan that day, with several targeting Atbara in River Nile State. The attack was repelled, the state police media office said . *** RSF looks to link positions in Blue Nile, launches attacks on military-held areas The RSF and its allies launched attacks on military positions across Blue Nile over two consecutive days, with the military repelling the assaults in Kurmuk and Bao. On Friday, the RSF attacked Keili in the Kurmuk locality in four successive waves after heavy artillery and drone strikes, a military source told Mada Masr. Military forces, supported by drones, repelled the assault, the source said. According to the source, the attack was intended to link RSF units along the Geisan axis with those in Kurmuk and open a supply corridor between its positions on the southeastern border with Ethiopia and its forces farther south near South Sudan. The military said it captured 16 equipped combat vehicles during the fighting. On Saturday, the RSF and the allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (Abdel Aziz al-Hilu) attacked Magagga in Bao locality, the source said. Military forces launched a counterattack and flanked the attackers, killing and wounding dozens of RSF fighters and capturing around six combat vehicles and several motorcycles, according to the source. The Fourth Infantry Division in Damazin, Blue Nile’s capital, said it also shot down a strategic drone carrying out reconnaissance over over Kurmuk on Saturday. *** US withholds Burhan’s visa for UN General Assembly as Sudan resists US truce terms Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem meets with UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres on the margins of the UN General Assembly, September 24. Photo: The Foreign Ministry via X. Diplomats and heads of state have flocked to New York this week to attend the senior meetings of the United Nations General Assembly, and Sudanese Transitional Council chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan was expected to be among them. The UNGA had put him down to deliver a speech on Thursday. But Burhan did not give that speech, and he did not travel to New York at all, because the United States declined to issue him a visa . Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem attended in his stead. Within Sudanese official circles, the denial was read as a pressure tactic aimed at the government’s resistance to a 90-day truce proposal that Washington is now pushing, several officials informed of preparations for the trip and crisis mediation tell Mada Masr. The possibility of the visa being withheld had already been factored into Sudan’s preparations, given the 2025 US sanctions on the TSC chair and military chief, but officials now see the move as part of the dispute over the truce proposal, which had come up in trilateral discussions earlier in the week. Burhan’s visa denial is the latest in a series of fractious interactions with the US administration in recent months over proposals for a humanitarian pause, ceasefire and pathway toward a postwar political settlement. While the international community coalesced around a power-sharing proposal following the fall of Fasher, the Sudanese government viewed re-entering into power with the RSF or accepting the de facto partition of Sudan as a non-starter and sought to undermine that consensus. In the year since, the international consensus has frayed even as the US continues to adhere to the same principle. Throughout that time, the Sudanese government has sought to open parallel, competing negotiating tracks to give itself greater room to resist arrangements the military believes would erode Sudan’s historic state institutions. Several proposals have been tabled, but amid the divide at home and internationally, none has gained significant traction and the fighting continues unabated. For Burhan, the issue is not US mediation itself, but the terms under which Washington would exercise that role. He “does not accept a US role based on directing the Sudanese government or imposing a political formula on it,” a source close to him said. Any outside role, the source added, should support a Sudanese negotiating process rather than replace it. Though this divergence in positions has come to define diplomacy around the war in Sudan, there was still a push to bridge the gap over the proposal and Burhan’s participation. On Sunday, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdel Atty and US Advisor on Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos met Salem to discuss the US proposal and whether it could be developed further, according to a Sudanese source involved in the communications around the meeting. Salem attended the meeting to hear out the proposal and discuss its details, particularly its implementation mechanisms, guarantees and the political process expected to follow the pause in fighting, the source said. The Sudanese side wanted a clear answer on “what comes after the 90 days,” he added, because that question lay at the core of the government’s reservations. According to another Sudanese source informed of the contacts, Burhan did not want the meeting or subsequent discussions to become a mechanism for imposing a political arrangement on Sudan. On Monday, the Sudanese mission to the UN approached the organization over the US failure to issue the visa. No official notice of denial had been issued, but Burhan was still without one. Sudan’s ambassador to the UN Al-Harith Idriss wrote to the secretary general seeking UN intervention to ensure Burhan could attend the General Assembly meetings, a Sudanese diplomatic source in New York told Mada Masr. The move followed direct contacts over the status of the visa, the source said. But the US was not prepared to back down and let its frustration be known. The next day, US State Department spokesperson Thomas Pigott issued a statement that gave the Sudanese government further reason to view the visa issue in political terms. “We have repeatedly asked [the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces] to accept a humanitarian truce as presented without preconditions, and to commit to an inclusive political dialogue that leads to a transition to a civilian government,” the statement read. “Regrettably, neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the Rapid Support Forces have made serious commitments to an immediate truce.” The statement went on to say that neither party to the war, nor their leaders, “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan — they rule through force of arms alone,” adding that their conduct renders them “ineligible to govern the country.” Following the statement, it was clear to the Sudanese government that the visa denial was not a consular matter, but was tied more directly to the political dispute over the US truce proposal and formed part of the broader disagreement with Washington over how the war should be handled, the diplomatic source in New York and a second Sudanese diplomatic source told Mada Masr. Khartoum had initially dealt with US contacts as a channel for negotiating an end to the fighting, the second source said, but linking those communications to conditions concerning Burhan’s participation in the General Assembly made the issue more sensitive for Sudan’s leadership. Burhan has not changed his position on the proposal, according to the source close to him. What Washington considers a precondition for his participation, the source said, is seen in Khartoum as an attempt to determine a political arrangement that should instead be negotiated. Sudan is prepared to discuss a 90-day truce, but Burhan wants changes to the proposal, along with clear guarantees and mechanisms for implementing and monitoring it. Khartoum wants to know what would happen during and after the truce. This includes whether the truce would cover all fronts and clarity on troop movements, the entry of weapons, redeployment, mechanisms for monitoring violations, humanitarian access and who would oversee the political phase that follows, the source said. Burhan is particularly opposed to what the source described as an “accept first, negotiate later” approach. The Sudanese government wants to discuss the proposal term by term before committing to it, the source said, because Burhan believes that accepting a truce without knowing what arrangements would follow could reproduce earlier ceasefires, when pauses in fighting were used to reposition military forces. Pigott’s characterization of the armed forces and the RSF as equivalent parties has raised another concern in Khartoum. The government distinguishes between demanding an end to the fighting and making a political characterization of the role of state institutions and the armed forces, the source said. The latter, he added, takes the dispute beyond the ceasefire and into the question of Sudan’s future system of government. That question is also at the heart of Khartoum’s reservations about Washington’s proposed “inclusive civilian dialogue,” a Sudanese Foreign Ministry source told Mada Masr. The government wants to know who would take part, how representation would be determined and how the dialogue would relate to existing state institutions. It rejects any arrangement that could create a parallel authority or give armed groups a political role derived from military force, the source said. That position is central to the government’s reservations about the political process that would follow any truce. The government has told its international partners that it does not regard the 90-day proposal as a final agreement, but as a document that needs to be discussed, the Sudanese Foreign Ministry source said. Amid the tensions, Sudan and its regional allies are stepping up their contacts. Abdel Atty met with Burhan’s advisor, Amgad Farid, in New York on Thursday, as part of Egypt’s contacts with Sudan’s leadership during the UNGA meetings, the second Sudanese diplomatic source said. The meeting covered developments in the war and ongoing international efforts to end it, according to the source, who said Cairo is working to keep a channel open with Burhan as tensions between Khartoum and Washington intensify. Saudi contacts with Burhan have also intensified in recent days, according to a Sudanese source informed of regional diplomacy, with Riyadh seeking to maintain direct communication with Sudan’s leadership as the dispute with Washington deepens. The talks are focused on the war, proposed options for ending it and preventing the disagreement over the US proposal from turning into a rupture between Khartoum and Washington. Khartoum sees its contacts with Cairo and Riyadh as part of a wider network of regional relationships through which it can operate at the current stage, particularly as Burhan’s trip to New York was held up, the source said. The government wants the discussion over the war to remain spread across regional and international channels rather than allowing Washington to become the sole channel setting the terms of a political settlement. Salem’s meetings in New York have served that purpose. He met UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres on Thursday and briefed him on developments in Sudan and the government’s position on humanitarian operations, a member of the Sudanese delegation said. The delay in issuing Burhan’s visa was also discussed. Guterres expressed regret over the disruption to Burhan’s participation, according to the source, who said the UN secretariat has continued contacts with US authorities over the matter. The Sudanese Foreign Ministry said Salem reiterated the government’s commitment to working with the secretary general’s personal envoy and with international and regional humanitarian organizations, as well as facilitating aid convoys and humanitarian access. The meeting also gave Salem an opportunity to explain the government’s position on proposals to end the war, another member of the Sudanese delegation told Mada Masr. In particular, he emphasized that any political arrangements that follow a truce should remain tied to state institutions and to a negotiating process in which Sudanese parties participate directly. Salem also held talks with African Union officials that day. Khartoum wants to preserve the AU’s role in any future process, the second Sudanese diplomatic source told Mada Masr, seeing it as a regional framework that could help address disagreements over the shape of a political settlement alongside US and UN diplomacy. For now, the source close to Burhan said, his position is to “open negotiating channels with everyone while rejecting preconditions.” Khartoum wants the war to end, he added, but the path to that outcome must run through arrangements agreed upon with the Sudanese government, preserving state institutions and clearly defining the political phase that will come after the fighting stops. *** South Sudan’s Kiir dissolves power-sharing govt, clears way for December vote South Sudanese President Salva Kiir and then-First Vice President Riek Machar in Juba after the first meeting of the transitional government, April 2016. Photo: AP Photo/Jason Patinkin. In the space of one week, South Sudanese President Salva Kiir moved rapidly to reshape the country’s electoral process, appointing a new elections commission chair, amending the electoral law and dissolving the transitional government, ahead of the country’s first general election since independence. The opposition rejected the amendments as a unilateral decision made without agreement among the parties to the 2018 peace deal, according to a leader in the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in Opposition. Led by former First Vice President Riek Machar, the movement is one of the main opponents of the agreement. Machar, who signed the deal, is currently on trial in Juba on charges including treason and murder. The changes allow the government to circumvent the transitional requirements as the country enters the final months before the December 22 vote. Yet many of the basic preparations remain incomplete, while the UN has warned that holding elections amid continued political and security instability without adequate safeguards could increase the risk of violence. The elections were meant to take place in 2024, but Kiir postponed them in what opposition sources previously described to Mada Masr as a maneuver to buy time to reconfigure the government and sideline Machar, who retains a strong support base, and other opposition-appointed officials. A succession of reshuffles, dismissals and security crackdowns followed, steadily hollowing out the power-sharing arrangements and culminating in Machar’s suspension as first vice president. By the time a date was set for the vote in June, the groundwork was in place. Kiir began the push on September 15 by changing the leadership of the National Elections Commission. He dismissed its chair, Abednego Akok Kacuol, and appointed the commission’s former secretary general, Gabriel Bol Deng Majok, in his place without justification. An opposition source called the move politically biased, saying electoral rules set specific grounds for removing the chair, including proven bias, inability to perform the job or serious misconduct. The abrupt change could also unsettle the commission as its new leadership gets up to speed and makes decisions on the electoral timetable, political analyst and journalist Atem Simon told Mada Masr. Then, on Monday, Kiir signed amendments to the 2012 National Elections Act, after the Transitional National Legislative Assembly approved them the same day. The changes remove two conditions for holding the election: completion of a permanent constitution and a population census A source in Kiir’s office hailed the amendments as “another important stage” in preparations for the election. The amendments gave Kiir the power to remove the vice presidents appointed under the peace agreement — which he exercised on Tuesday when he dissolved the transitional government. The decree also dismissed ministers and local administrators, leaving Kiir in the presidency and dismantling much of the power-sharing arrangement around him. His advisors were left in place. A large deployment of security and military forces was reported in Juba on the day the dissolution announcement was made. In a directive viewed by Agence France-Presse, the Internal Security Bureau ordered all forces to be “on high alert” for three days starting September 22. Kiir’s successive moves came as the parties to the peace deal were still waiting to hold a dialogue they had agreed to establish in December 2025 to discuss the electoral changes and other issues surrounding the vote, an opposition source said. The talks, originally scheduled for the previous week, were postponed to September 24. Kiir opened the sessions, and urged political forces to keep the discussions focused on electoral matters and not use the dialogue to renegotiate the electoral process. The sessions are slated to run for two weeks. The dialogue is supposed to settle disagreements over the constitutional and legal basis for the election, political freedoms, the role of the parties and the future of the peace agreement, Simon told Mada Masr. It should also determine how parties that have reservations about the current process will participate. The concern, he said, is that the dialogue could end up being cosmetic — a way of giving political cover to decisions already made rather than a genuine negotiation. The dialogue would only matter if the parties can reach an agreement on the rules and guarantees of the vote. Moreover, the government appears politically determined to reach the election, but it is not equally prepared on the technical and institutional fronts, he said. Voter registration has not yet begun, leaving the country without a voter roll or an official estimate of the number of eligible voters, with the elections commission still training registration officials, a source in the commission told Mada Mada. Questions over funding, security, electoral constituencies and the political and media environment remain unresolved, Simon said. If those basic conditions cannot be met before December 22, the parties should be transparent about it rather than rush through a contested election, he added. A vote held under those circumstances could deepen the political crisis instead of bringing the transition to an end. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan warned last month that holding elections without a strategy to consolidate democracy and prevent further political divisions could instead fuel renewed conflict and increase the risk of atrocity crimes. “Armed conflict has resumed in several parts of the country; inclusive politics being abandoned; civic space and constitutional safeguards have been weakened; accountability mechanisms remain largely absent; and significant sections of the population remain excluded from meaningful political participation,” it said. “Without a return to genuine and inclusive dialogue, the political contest surrounding the elections risks deepening existing divisions rather than providing a peaceful means of resolving them.” For Simon, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development could play an important role in calling for and supporting such dialogue. The regional bloc sponsored the 2018 peace agreement and has direct experience with the complexities of South Sudan’s political crisis, he said. An IGAD-backed dialogue could help bring the government and parties to the agreement together, particularly as trust has declined and disagreements have intensified over the elections and the implementation of the remaining provisions of the peace deal, he added. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . items.title: Government repatriates 180 Ghanaians from Libya
items.description: The Government of Ghana, in collaboration with the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), has facilitated the safe return of 180 Ghanaian nationals from Libya. According to a post from Ministry of Foreign Affairs Facebook page, the repatriation took place on Thursday, September 24, 2026, as part of ongoing efforts to assist vulnerable Ghanaians stranded abroad or seeking to return home. The returnees comprised 153 males and 27 females, including children and infants. Upon their arrival in Ghana, the returnees were received by the Resident Representative of ECOWAS in Ghana, H.E. Mohammed Lawan Gana, officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and representatives of the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO). The officials welcomed the returnees and expressed appreciation to the institutions and partners involved in facilitating their safe return. In his remarks, H.E. Mohammed Lawan Gana assured the returnees that their safe arrival marked an important step towards rebuilding their lives. He encouraged them not to view their return as a setback but as an opportunity to make a fresh start. He also urged the returnees to remain hopeful and make constructive use of the support available to them. He encouraged them to explore opportunities in skills development, entrepreneurship and other livelihood programmes that could support their reintegration into their communities. The repatriation forms part of continued cooperation between the Government of Ghana, IOM and ECOWAS to support the voluntary return and reintegration of Ghanaian nationals in vulnerable situations abroad. The initiative also reflects the commitment of the institutions to promoting safe, orderly and regular migration, while ensuring that Ghanaian nationals who require assistance can return home safely and receive the necessary support to reintegrate into society. The returnees are expected to receive appropriate assistance as they begin the reintegration process, with the relevant authorities and partner organisations continuing to work together to support their transition and wellbeing.

items.title: GNAT demands independent probe into death of teacher at Gindabour
items.description: The Northern Regional Executives of the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT) are demanding an independent and transparent investigation into the death of a teacher, Abu Seidu, following an encounter with police personnel at Gindabour in the Savannah Region. GNAT says the Ghana Police Service should not be allowed to be the sole investigator in an incident in which its personnel are alleged to have been directly involved. Mr Seidu, a professional teacher at Gindabour D/A Primary School in the Sawla-Tuna-Kalba District, died on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, in circumstances that remain disputed. In a statement issued on September 24, the Northern Regional GNAT Executives said the investigation must establish exactly what happened from the moment Mr Seidu encountered the police until his death. “This is precisely why GNAT demands an independent investigation. The Police Service cannot be allowed to be the sole investigator of an incident in which its own personnel are alleged to have been directly involved,” the union said. GNAT said where a citizen dies following an encounter with law-enforcement officers, the circumstances must be subjected to an investigation that is “independent, impartial, transparent and credible enough to command public confidence.” The union’s demand comes amid differing accounts of the circumstances surrounding Mr Seidu’s death. The Police Service has said officers on patrol encountered a motorbike rider who diverted into the bush after seeing their vehicle. The officers reportedly later found him unconscious and began conveying him to hospital, but he died on the way. Community accounts, however, have raised questions about what happened between the encounter with the police and the teacher’s death. The bodies of Mr Seidu and General Constable Redeemer Owusu, who was later killed in a mob attack, were taken for preservation and autopsy. GNAT is also calling for the autopsy findings on Mr Seidu to form part of the independent investigation and for the outcome to be communicated transparently to his family and the public, subject to applicable legal requirements. The union further wants a separate investigation into the death of General Constable Owusu, stressing that it condemns mob justice, vigilantism and the unlawful killing of any person. “Justice for Abu Seidu must not be pursued at the expense of justice for Redeemer Owusu, and justice for Redeemer Owusu must not be pursued at the expense of justice for Abu Seidu,” GNAT said. The union has also demanded an independent inquiry into allegations of vandalism, destruction of property, assault and intimidation allegedly committed during subsequent security operations in Gindabour. GNAT said if such allegations are established, those responsible must be held accountable, stressing that the State’s responsibility is to restore order and not punish an entire community. “Collective punishment has no place in a constitutional democracy,” the union said.

items.title: Mark Carney says he has considered possibility of US military action against Canada
items.description: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has considered the remote possibility of US military action against Canada, according to an interview with The New York Times. Carney told the Times that his administration has carefully examined the “extreme tail risk” scenario where the US takes military action against his country, and had prepared accordingly, without providing further detail. “I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told the Times. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare. Tensions between the neighbouring countries have flared under US President Donald Trump. Any conflict would likely be highly imbalanced. The US military has more than 2 million active-duty and reserve troops, while Canada has fewer than 200,000, according to their governments. Similarly, as of 2024, the US possessed 65 military submarines, compared to Canada’s four. Canada, though, has the longest coastline in the world and is close to the Arctic, two circumstances that have prompted Carney to boost defence spending since he took office. Meanwhile, Trump has frequently talked about Canada as the “51st state”. He also started a trade war with it that deepened last month as the two countries began exchanging tit-for-tat tariffs on a number of products. Even since then, Carney told the Times, he speaks with Trump “frequently”. “From my perspective, we have a good relationship in the sense of we can pick up the phone and talk to each other about issues,” he told the outlet. “He’s direct. I’m direct in terms of where positions are. It’s much more efficient that way, and so you know that exists and that will continue to exist.” Carney said he believed there was still a path to resume trade negotiations with the US. Returning to their amicable ties would be beneficial for both countries, he said.

items.title: Gindabour: GNAT demands GES statement on death of teacher
items.description: The Northern Regional Executives of the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT) has expressed disappointment in the Ghana Education Service (GES) for failing to issue a formal public statement on the death of teacher Abu Seidu at Gindabour. According to them, the apparent silence from the GES was troubling, particularly because Mr Seidu was an employee of the Service. In a statement issued September 24, GNAT said: “The Northern Regional GNAT executives are particularly disappointed by the apparent absence, as of the date of this statement, of a formal public statement from the Ghana Education Service (GES) condemning the death of Mr. Abu Seidu and expressing solidarity with his bereaved family and colleagues.” The Association stressed that the circumstances surrounding the teacher’s death had generated national concern and competing accounts, making it necessary for his employer to publicly respond. “When a teacher dies in circumstances that have generated national concern and competing accounts, the employer cannot afford to remain silent,” GNAT said. It added: “Silence in the face of the death of a member of the teaching profession is deeply troubling.” GNAT has therefore called on the GES to immediately formally acknowledge the death of Mr Seidu and express condolences to his family and colleagues. The Association also wants the Service to “publicly condemn any unlawful conduct established to have contributed to his death” and cooperate fully with an independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident. It further called on the GES to provide “appropriate institutional support to the bereaved family.” Mr Seidu, a teacher at Gindabour D/A Primary School, died following an encounter involving police officers in the area. His death was followed by the killing of General Constable Redeemer Owusu, amid heightened tensions in the community. (MyJoyOnline⁠￼) GNAT said the GES must demonstrate institutional responsibility towards one of its employees while the circumstances surrounding his death are investigated.

items.title: 6th Western Gospel Awards unveils nominees ahead of November ceremony
items.description: The 6th Western Gospel Awards has unveiled nominees for the 2026 edition, with the main ceremony scheduled for Saturday, 14 November. The ceremony will take place at the Western Serene Atlantic Hotel in Ghana and is expected to attract gospel artistes, music executives, media personalities, clergy, industry professionals, fans and other stakeholders for a night celebrating excellence and contribution to gospel music. Organised by Prolific GH, the Western Gospel Awards has established itself as a platform dedicated to recognising the talents, ministries, creatives and industry contributors helping to advance gospel music, particularly in the Western and Western North regions. Speaking on preparations for this year’s ceremony, Lead Consultant of the Western Gospel Awards, Mr Maxwell Bills Ghansah, officially confirmed the date and venue for the 2026 edition. The announcement sets the stage for what organisers say will be another major gathering of gospel music personalities and stakeholders. The awards will celebrate nominees across several areas of the gospel music industry, highlighting both established names and emerging talents. Adding to the event, organisers have named renowned event host and master of ceremonies Nana Quasi-Owusu, popularly known as PM TheFinest, as the official host for the 6th edition. He is expected to steer proceedings throughout the ceremony as winners are announced and nominees, artistes and other industry contributors receive recognition for their work. The 2026 nominees represent a wide range of talents and contributions within Ghana’s gospel music ecosystem. Categories include gospel artistes, songwriters, vocalists, music events, music videos, radio and television programmes, collaborations, among other areas of recognition. The organisers are calling on fans, churches, gospel music lovers and industry stakeholders to support the nominees and follow the official Western Gospel Awards platforms for updates as the November ceremony approaches. The 6th edition of the Western Gospel Awards is expected to bring together some of the industry’s established voices alongside emerging talents, creating a platform for recognition, networking and celebration. As preparations intensify, the Western Serene Atlantic Hotel will host the ceremony on 14 November 2026, for an evening dedicated to celebrating the people and works contributing to the growth of gospel music. items.title: GMTF, GNPC open talks on stronger support for specialised healthcare
items.description: The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) is exploring a strategic partnership with the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) to mobilise additional support for healthcare infrastructure and specialised medical services across the country. The discussions between the two institutions are aimed at identifying areas where their collaboration could help address critical needs within Ghana’s health sector, particularly in improving medical support systems and expanding access to specialised care. The engagement forms part of the GMTF’s broader strategy of working with major institutions to mobilise resources for interventions that can directly benefit patients and strengthen healthcare facilities. Potential areas of cooperation include support for healthcare infrastructure and medical services, with the two institutions examining how a partnership could contribute to improving the capacity of facilities to provide quality care. The discussions also come as the GMTF marks its first year of operations, providing an opportunity for the Fund to deepen its institutional partnerships as it enters what it describes as a new phase of expanded interventions in the health sector. The Fund has been pursuing partnerships with institutions and stakeholders as part of efforts to complement existing healthcare resources and respond to identified needs in medical facilities and among patients. A collaboration with GNPC could provide another avenue for mobilising resources and expertise for healthcare interventions, particularly in areas requiring significant investment in infrastructure and specialised medical support. The engagement underscores the growing focus on strategic partnerships as the GMTF seeks to broaden its reach and contribute to stronger healthcare delivery across Ghana.

items.title: Éliminatoires CAN 2027 : les Lions de Vieira accrochés à Maputo
items.description: Pour ses grands débuts sur le banc des Lions, Patrick Vieira n'a pas connu l'entame rêvée. Le Sénégal a été tenu en échec par le Mozambique (1-1), ce jeudi à Maputo, lors de la première journée des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Longtemps maîtres du jeu, les Champions d'Afrique en titre avaient pourtant idéalement lancé leur campagne grâce à un but de Nicolas Jackson, auteur d'une première période solide et aboutie. Mais juste avant la pause, coup de tonnerre du côté des Mambas : sur une frappe enroulée depuis l'extérieur de la surface, le Mozambique surprend Yehvann Diouf, semble-t-il gêné dans sa vision, et arrache l'égalisation au meilleur moment. Ce but concédé à la limite de la mi-temps a visiblement pesé sur le moral des Lions. Au retour des vestiaires, Patrick Vieira a multiplié les changements pour tenter de relancer les siens, faisant entrer Ibrahima Mbaye à la place de Pape Matar Sarr à la 62ᵉ minute, avant de lancer également Boulaye Dia et Pape Moussa dans la bataille. Mais rien n'y a fait : la seconde période a été bien pâle côté sénégalais, l'équipe peinant à se procurer la moindre occasion franche et donnant l'image d'un groupe collectivement démobilisé après le coup dur encaissé juste avant la pause. Un point du nul, donc, pour l'entame de l'ère Vieira, qui devra vite trouver les solutions pour redresser la barre. Les partenaires de Pape Gueye enchaîneront dès mardi, à 15h, avec un déplacement à Addis-Abeba pour y affronter l'Éthiopie, dans ce groupe J où le Soudan a pris les commandes après sa victoire à domicile face aux Éthiopiens (1-0). Une position de leader qui relègue provisoirement le Sénégal et le Mozambique à la deuxième place, l'Éthiopie fermant la marche sans le moindre point. Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: Forum des cultures unies à Saint-Pétersbourg : Vladimir Poutine insiste sur le dialogue, la diversité et la coopération culturelle internationale
items.description: Vladimir Poutine a participe ce 25 septembre au XIIe Forum international des cultures unies a Saint-Petersbourg. Dans son intervention, le president russe a place la culture au cœur des relations entre les peuples, estimant qu'elle pouvait preserver le dialogue meme lorsque d'autres formes de cooperation sont interrompues. « La culture est capable de construire des ponts entre les personnes malgre toutes les contradictions », a declare Vladimir Poutine. Il a souligne qu'elle demeurait un moyen de communication « la ou les liens politiques et economiques sont geles » en raison de desaccords, de sanctions ou de restrictions. Selon lui, les echanges culturels permettent ainsi de maintenir des points de convergence malgre les tensions et les divisions. Le forum reunit cette annee des representants d'environ 70 pays, dont 44 delegations officielles. Placee sous le theme « Cultures unies – valeurs communes », cette douzieme edition rassemble responsables, artistes et professionnels du secteur autour de plusieurs dizaines de rencontres consacrees aux echanges et a la cooperation culturelle. Diversite russe, jeunesse et nouvelles technologies Le president russe a egalement relie cette conception du dialogue a l'histoire et a la diversite de la Russie. Il a rappele que le pays s'etait construit comme un espace reunissant differents peuples, langues et traditions. Selon Vladimir Poutine, l'unite russe ne repose pas sur l'uniformite, mais sur une cohesion fondee sur le developpement propre de chaque peuple et de chaque groupe ethnique. Il a par ailleurs declare que « l'art veritable », classique comme contemporain, appartient a tous. Les valeurs communes doivent, a-t-il souligne, constituer des points d'appui sans conduire a l'imposition d'une vision unique. La jeunesse occupe egalement une place importante dans cette approche. Vladimir Poutine a estime que les jeunes contribuent a maintenir le dialogue culturel entre les pays et a developper de nouvelles formes de cooperation. Il a dans le meme temps insiste sur la necessite de rapprocher traditions et technologies, notamment grâce a la numerisation de fonds audio et d'archives locales afin de preserver une « histoire vivante ». Des initiatives russes ouvertes a l'international Le chef de l'etat a egalement presente plusieurs experiences developpees en Russie et susceptibles d'etre adaptees dans d'autres pays. Parmi elles figure la « Carte Pouchkine », un dispositif destine a faciliter l'acces des jeunes aux institutions culturelles. Vladimir Poutine a explique que ce modele numerique pouvait etre adapte a differents contextes en modifiant le montant attribue, l'âge des beneficiaires ou la liste des etablissements concernes. Le principe resterait cependant inchange : assurer un acces direct a la culture et preserver la liberte de choix. Le president russe a egalement appele a mieux recenser et diffuser les initiatives qui ont fait leurs preuves dans le secteur culturel, notamment a travers une base regroupant transcriptions, videos, commentaires et entretiens issus du forum. Il a parallelement insiste sur la formation de professionnels capables de maîtriser a la fois les enjeux artistiques, les attentes du public et les nouvelles technologies. Enfin, Vladimir Poutine a salue le developpement de l'Academie eurasienne des arts cinematographiques ainsi que du prix « Papillon de diamant » dans le cadre des BRICS. Il a reaffirme a cette occasion l'ouverture de la Russie a une cooperation culturelle etroite et au developpement des echanges avec ses partenaires internationaux.

items.title: Super Falcons defender Osinachi Ohale retires from international football
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Super Falcons defender, Osinachi Ohale, has announced her retirement from international football after 16 years of representing Nigeria. Ohale made the announcement in a statement shared on her official Instagram handle on Friday, bringing an end to a national-team career in which she earned 86 caps and represented Nigeria at four FIFA Women’s World Cups and seven Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) tournaments. “After 16 years of wearing the Nigerian jersey, representing my country, and giving everything I had to the beautiful game, I have made the very difficult decision to retire from international football,” Ohale said. The 34-year-old defender reflected on her journey from dreaming of playing for Nigeria to becoming a five-time WAFCON champion. “I can only look back with a heart overflowing with gratitude,” she said. Ohale was part of the Super Falcons teams that won five WAFCON titles and featured prominently across several major international tournaments. Reflecting on her career, the defender said the memories of representing Nigeria would remain with her beyond the statistics and trophies. “I have stood on the biggest stages in the world, representing Nigeria at four FIFA Women’s World Cups and seven WAFCON, and I am incredibly proud that we lifted the African title five times,” she said. “But beyond the numbers and trophies are the memories that will stay with me forever — the tears, the celebrations, the difficult moments, the victories, the defeats, the friendships, the sacrifices, and every time I stood proudly with my hand over my heart and heard the Nigerian anthem.” Ohale also thanked her teammates, coaches, support staff, family, friends and the Nigeria Football Federation for being part of her journey. “To my teammates, coaches, staff, family, friends, Nigeria Football Federation and everyone who walked this journey with me — thank you,” she said. The defender, who plays for Mexican Liga MX Femenil club Pachuca Femenil, also expressed appreciation to Nigerian fans for their support throughout her international career. “To the Nigerian fans: thank you for believing in us, supporting us, celebrating with us, and standing by us through every high and every low. Your love made wearing this jersey even more special,” she added. View this post on Instagram Ohale said she was leaving international football without regrets, describing her opportunity to represent Nigeria as her greatest achievement. “Today, I say goodbye to international football with no regrets — only gratitude. “86 caps. 16 years. 4 World Cups. 7 WAFCON. 5 WAFCON titles. But the greatest achievement of all is knowing that I had the privilege to serve my country.” She concluded her statement with an emotional message to Nigeria, saying her retirement would not diminish her connection with the country. “The jersey will leave my shoulders, but it will never leave my heart. Thank you, Nigeria, for allowing me to live my dream.” “Forever a Super Falcon. Forever Nigerian,” Ohale said. items.title: Spirit & Truth: Nights of Revival returns to Accra on 27 September
items.description: Spirit & Truth: Nights of Revival, the monthly worship gathering led by Ghanaian pastor, worship minister and musician Barry Neequaye, will hold its next edition on Sunday, 27 September 2026, at 5:00pm at the L’aine Office Complex (3rd Floor), Adabraka, Accra. The evening is open to all who desire a deeper, more intentional encounter with God. At a time when worship gatherings can easily slip into routine, Spirit & Truth offers believers a deliberate space to slow down and seek God. Each edition brings worshippers together for an extended season of worship, prayer and spiritual reflection, placing the presence of God, rather than a fixed programme, at the centre of the night. The gathering is built on a simple conviction that shapes its atmosphere: that there is something significant about sitting at God’s feet and ministering to Him. In the ministry’s own words, “There’s nothing like sitting at God’s feet and ministering to Him.” Attendees are invited not simply to listen to music, but to participate fully in worship, prayer and the pursuit of God. The September edition builds on strong momentum from previous gatherings. Following the May edition, Kingdom Vessels described the night as one marked by “worship, prayer and deep encounters,” and thanked all who gathered, served, prayed and worshipped. Participants shared that they left in awe of what God had done “in our midst,” with many expressing anticipation for the next gathering. Rather than positioning each night as a standalone event on the Christian calendar, the ministry presents Spirit & Truth as a continuing journey, with each month’s gathering building expectation for the next. Bringing together Barry Neequaye’s music, the Word and fellowship in one recurring experience, Spirit & Truth: Nights of Revival is establishing itself as a regular meeting point in Accra for worshippers seeking a renewed focus on God’s presence.

items.title: Wike to lead Tinubu 2027 re-election campaign in FCT, Rivers
items.description: Minister, Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has announced plans to inaugurate and lead the campaign machinery in Abuja and Rivers to drive the re-election bid of President Bola Tinubu. Wike disclosed this in Abuja on Friday, after he inspected the ongoing Kuje-Gwagwalada road dualisation project. He added that he would lead the campaign effort within the nation’s capital and extend the re-election operations to his home state of Rivers. According to him, political parties across the spectrum are organising their ranks, and supporters of the president are prepared to initiate an aggressive campaign. “The ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), I believe, is putting itself together for an aggressive campaign. “For us who are supporting Mr President from different political platforms, we have put our machinery ready to kick-start. “Very soon, I will inaugurate the campaign team for Tinubu in the FCT and Rivers, which I will lead. “All elements of the APC are ready, Mr President is ready, we are ready and you can see the enthusiasm.” Addressing critics and political opponents, Wike argued that visible development projects would serve as the main driver for electoral support in the FCT, dismissing allegations of electoral malpractice ahead of time. “People are happy, and I don’t know who will contest against the president as far as this election is concerned. “This is governance, and this is what people expect. It will translate directly into actual votes,” he said. Wike expressed confidence that the administration’s infrastructure record would secure victory across board in the FCT, including support for Sen. Philip Aduda and the two House of Representatives seats. “It is obvious. Nobody will be able to claim rigging in FCT. The ‘rigging’ is the projects we are delivering, making the people happy,” Wike said. Commending the contractor and site engineers for the progress recorded so far, the minister assured stakeholders that adequate funding would be disbursed to guarantee completion of the project by December. “This is my first time getting to this side of the road, and I can see how highly populated this area is,” he said. The minister emphasised that delivering functional infrastructure remains the cornerstone of good governance and public satisfaction. “You can imagine the enthusiasm and happiness on the faces of the people. That is why we say the essence of governance is to make people happy. “When the people are happy, those in authority are happy,” he added, expressing gratitude to Tinubu for providing sustained support for capital projects in the territory. items.title: Gold exporters accuse influential actors of draining Sudan’s gold wealth
items.description: Sudan’s Gold Exporters Division has accused influential actors of taking gold outside official channels, warning that the country is losing billions of dollars in potential revenue while the pound continues to slide. Sudan produces more than 70 tonnes of gold a year worth an estimated $8 billion, but only about $2 billion reaches the state treasury, according to Abdelmoneim Siddig, head of the Gold Exporters Division. In an interview with Radio Dabanga today, Siddig said gold could help Sudan tackle its economic crisis and provide much-needed foreign currency but alleged that influential entities export gold outside formal channels. He accused the Central Bank of Sudan of buying gold at high prices, saying the practice encourages exports outside official channels and puts further pressure on the Sudanese pound. Siddig said smuggled gold becomes a source of foreign currency for travellers, students, patients and others, adding that rising gold prices drive up the dollar price and weaken the pound. He warned that weak oversight and flawed economic policies could deepen the crisis, leaving citizens to bear the cost through higher living expenses and deteriorating healthcare and education. “If these policies are not reversed, these government institutions that work unconsciously and care about nothing but to get any amount of dollars regardless of their economic consequences, will cause the crisis to worsen,” he said. Mining companies threaten halt The comments come as Sudan’s mining companies escalate their dispute with the government over the Central Bank’s gold purchasing and pricing mechanism. The Union of Mining Companies in Sudan has threatened to halt gold production from October 1, warning that the current system is making it difficult for companies to meet their financial and operational obligations. The union said companies recognise the state’s right to regulate the sector and collect its legal revenues, but reject the current mechanism for purchasing, pricing and settling payments for their production. The dispute centres on how the Central Bank buys companies’ gold, sets its value and settles their dues. Producers want a mechanism that better reflects gold’s economic value and production costs. Central Bank changes rules The Central Bank recently amended rules governing gold produced from m i ning waste after 23 companies warned they would gradually suspend production at the end of September before halting completely in October. New rules allow mining waste companies to sell their entire production to the Central Bank, authorised buyers or exporters. They can also hold export proceeds in foreign currency for up to 21 working days and use them for operational imports or other permitted obligations. The Central Bank ordered banks not to process gold exports by mining waste companies without its written approval and confirmation that all other requirements had been met. items.title: Adu-Boahene case: Atta Akyea files no-case submission, cites evidential gaps and failure to call material witnesses
items.description: Lead counsel for former National Signals Bureau (NSB) Director-General Kwabena Adu-Boahene, Samuel Atta Akyea, has filed a submission of no case to answer. He is citing alleged evidential gaps, inconsistencies and the prosecution’s failure to call material witnesses. The submission was filed after the prosecution closed its case in the trial involving Mr Adu-Boahene, his wife Angela Adjei-Boateng and another accused person. The defence contends that the evidence presented by the prosecution does not establish a sufficient case requiring the accused persons to open their defence. A key issue raised by the defence is the prosecution’s handling of evidence surrounding the alleged misuse of GH¢49.1 million earmarked for a cybersecurity project. The State alleges that the money was transferred through three cheques from an account associated with National Security into an account belonging to BNC Communications Bureau Limited, a company linked to the accused persons. The prosecution has further alleged that the funds were subsequently diverted and used for purposes unrelated to the intended cybersecurity procurement. The defence, however, has challenged aspects of the prosecution’s evidence, including the circumstances surrounding the transactions and the extent to which the disputed funds can be directly traced to assets and expenditure attributed to the accused persons. Mr Akyea has also pointed to what the defence considers inconsistencies in the evidence presented by prosecution witnesses. Another key argument concerns the failure to call what the defence considers material witnesses whose evidence, it argues, could have shed light on the management and authorisation of the funds. The defence has previously raised questions about the absence of senior officials connected to the National Security arrangements surrounding the disputed transactions. The prosecution’s final witness, EOCO investigator Frank Marshall Cromwell, was subjected to extensive cross-examination by Mr Akyea before the State closed its case. During the proceedings, the defence questioned the investigation into the alleged cybersecurity procurement and whether sufficient steps had been taken to independently establish that the project had not been delivered. The defence also challenged aspects of the financial investigation, including the tracing of funds and the basis for linking particular transactions and assets to the GH¢49.1 million. The prosecution, for its part, maintains that it has presented sufficient evidence to support the charges against the accused persons. The State has relied on financial records, bank statements and other documentary evidence to establish its case concerning the alleged diversion and use of the funds. Mr Adu-Boahene and the other accused persons have pleaded not guilty to the charges. The charges include stealing, conspiracy to steal, defrauding by false pretences, wilfully causing financial loss to the state, using public office for profit and money laundering. Following the filing of the no-case submission, the Attorney-General has been given 14 days to respond. The defence will subsequently have an opportunity to reply to the prosecution’s response before the court determines whether the accused persons have a case to answer. A ruling on the no-case submission is expected to determine whether the trial proceeds to the defence stage or whether the accused persons are discharged.

items.title: Gov Otti rules out presidency, elective office after Abia tenure
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, has ruled out seeking the presidency or any other elective office after completing his tenure as governor, saying he would retire from politics. Otti made this known in an interview with Arise TV on Friday while responding to questions on former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi’s presidential ambition and whether he would consider seeking the presidency in the future. “I had said just a few days ago that by the time I’m done with this, I’ll retire. So I’m not going to run for any other thing, not local government chairman, not Senate, not president, no,” Otti said. The governor said he was focused on fulfilling what he described as his calling in Abia, adding that he would leave politics after completing his tenure. “I think I came to deliver a calling, and that is what I’m doing now. Once I finish it, I’ll retire. And I’m not getting any younger anymore,” he added. Otti also dismissed any suggestion of a disagreement between him and Obi, saying the former governor would be free to campaign in Abia if he chose to do so. “Oh, absolutely. Anybody that wants to campaign in my state will be allowed. Peter Obi and I are not fighting. Just like there’s nobody I’m fighting. “So if he wants to campaign in the state, he will be allowed to campaign. If any other person, even Atiku, if he wants to campaign, he will be allowed to campaign. So that is what democracy is about,” he said. items.description: Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, sources have told BBC Sport. The Athletic is reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding them guilty of all but one count. Sources have told BBC Sport a decision has been made in the case, and City have been found guilty of the majority of breaches. The Premier League declined to comment. Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way. Instead they released a statement saying that the “Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality”. “The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence,” it added. BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of a defeat, Manchester City will appeal against the findings.

items.title: Info ministry dismisses Afghan claims of destroying Pakistani post near border in Balochistan as 'fake'
items.description: The information ministry dismissed on Friday claims by the Afghan defence ministry of a Pakistani post having been destroyed near the Spin Boldak border — the frontier between Balochistan and Kandahar — as “fake and fabricated”. The information ministry also took note of Afghan claims that there had been no casualties among the Afghan forces in the latest episode of clash between the two sides. “The claim is fake and fabricated. As per actual facts, an attempted Afghan aggression in the Gulistan sector was thwarted on night between Sept 24 and Sept 25, and during the process and subsequent heavy punishment inflicted on opposing Taliban posts, at least 13 Afghan Taliban personnel were killed and several injured,” the information ministry said in a post on X. It also shared visuals in the post, which the ministry said were of the incident. The incident, it added, had already been “widely covered by media and circulated extensively across social media, providing visual evidence of the border engagement and punishment inflicted on the Afghan Taliban after their cowardly attack”. “The […] Afghan ministry’s attempt is no surprise since the Taliban are habitual liars having no moral and reputational standing,” it added. The latest clash has taken place amid an uptick in tensions at the Pak-Afghan border. Pakistan conducted precision aerial and drone strikes in 10 locations across Afghanistan on Thursday in retaliation for drones launched from the neighbouring country a day earlier. The response came after eight drones, launched from Afghanistan, entered Pakistani airspace near the Torkham border and Kohat on Wednesday. Security sources said they were subsequently shot down. It was also reported that the Afghan Taliban engaged in unprovoked firing the night before near Kurram as security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to cross into Pakistan. On Sept 21, Pakistan, in response to recent terrorist attacks in KP, conducted “calibrated” airstrikes in the border region with Afghanistan against terrorist hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organisations. A statement from the information ministry on Monday said that over 28 terrorists were eliminated in the strikes. “It is a matter of grave concern that Afghanistan continues to remain a hub of terrorism,” the ministry said at the time, specifying that the “threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan”. The airstrikes had come after a major attack in the old Police Lines in KP’s Kohat claimed 23 lives and injured about 100 others. Eight terrorists were killed during an overnight clearance operation launched to clear the area. Ghazab lil-Haq Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described Monday’s action as part of Pakistan’s ongoing counter-terrorism campaign, Ghazab lil Haq. On the night of February 26, following unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban from across the border, Pakistan launched Operation Ghazab lil Haq against terrorist hideouts. Pakistan also carried out strikes in the border region with Afghanistan in late June , with the government saying they were in response to a wave of terrorist attacks, including one on a Rangers camp in Karachi . At the time, Tarar said that 25 terrorists were killed in those strikes in Paktia, Paktika and Kunar. Pakistan had carried out similar strikes on terrorist hideouts along its border with Afghanistan earlier that month, killing 26 terrorists. In July, security forces responded to unprovoked firing by the Afghan Taliban at border posts in Kurram, security sources had said. In the same month, the Afghan Taliban regime launched four rudimentary drones across the border into Balochistan, which were shot down by security forces. Two drones were also shot down in June in Qila Abdullah and Chagai districts. Pak-Afghan ties As clashes continue, tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have remained high. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. Earlier this week, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar addressed a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), where he called for steps towards concrete and verifiable action to prevent the use of Afghan soil for terrorism against any neighbouring country, particularly Pakistan. Dar said Pakistan was “seriously concerned” about the presence of over two dozen terrorist groups in Afghanistan that threatened regional and international peace and security. Last week, Pakistan also told the UN Security Council that it would respond to terrorist threats emanating from Afghanistan in self-defence as and when needed and in accordance with international law. Earlier this month, the Foreign Office (FO) declared that meaningful progress in relations with Kabul would depend on the Taliban taking concrete and verifiable action against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and other terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory. It maintained that while Islamabad welcomed China’s continuing engagement, the external facilitation could not substitute for action by Kabul against terrorist infrastructure. According to a UN Security Council-mandated monitoring report — covering the period from December 16, 2025 to June 9, 2026 — Afg­han Taliban’s continued support for TTP has contributed to a rise in the frequency and lethality of terrorist attacks in Pakistan, even as Kabul has taken some initial steps to rein in the group. The report also pointed to growing operational and facilitation linkages among the TTP, Al Qaeda, Islamic State-Khorasan (ISIL-K) and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).
