items.title: Why Macklemore Was Kicked Off the Ed Sheeran Tour
items.description: Among the many reckonings sparked after the rapper Macklemore was booted from Ed Sheeran’s tour earlier this month, one of the more amusing ones has been about taste. Macklemore, who’d gotten ejected after saying “Free Palestine” onstage, is widely seen as a goofy mascot of Millennial cringe. Sheeran, who put out a statement declining to share his personal views on “this devastating conflict” and then continued his tour, is a folk-pop singer beloved at children’s birthday parties. Now some pro-Palestine music fans are joking that “Thrift Shop,” Macklemore’s saxophone-skronked 2012 hit, isn’t as annoying as they’d thought. As for Sheeran, his bland songwriting is serving as a rhetorical piñata. “This crisis is the worst thing that has happened to Ed Sheeran fans since their head injury,” sniped a comedian on Saturday Night Live UK . Political allegiances and artistic quality don’t actually correlate, but it does make sense that music’s most consequential confrontation over Israel and Palestine has been driven by two of the least cool people in all of popular culture. Precisely because they’re perceived to have little edge or relevance, Sheeran and Macklemore offered a perfect test case for questions about whether popular music is expected to change the world or distract from it, rebel against the system or serve the man—and who exactly sets those expectations. The situation began earlier this month when the 43-year-old Macklemore gave speeches centered on the phrase “Free Palestine” while opening for Sheeran at two shows in New Jersey. “I want those words to be loud and clear, so the people from Gaza all the way to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten them,” he said. He also played “Hind’s Hall,” a 2024 track that accuses Israel of genocide and voices support for pro-Palestinian campus protesters in the U.S. Imagery of those protests and the destruction in Gaza played on screens behind him. Groups such as the Anti-Defamation League and StopAntisemitism quickly issued criticism calling Macklemore bigoted and—to quote a petition from the Israeli-American Council—“biased.” In a lengthy post, the musician Pink wrote that Macklemore had caused her to feel fear “as a Jewish mom.” Much of the outcry connected Macklemore’s performance to an incident in 2014 in which he caused offense by wearing a costume that looked an awful lot like a Jewish caricature. At the time, the rapper apologized and said he’d disguised himself with random props without realizing the implications of how he looked. The backlash then was loud but died down relatively quickly, and the ADL said that it “accepted Macklemore at his word.” This time, the billionaire Robert Kraft, who co-owns Gillette Stadium, in Massachusetts, called Sheeran to say that he wouldn’t allow Macklemore to play his venue and that neither would a number of other stadium owners. On September 14, the rapper was dropped from the billing. Shortly after that, all of the tour’s other opening acts, plus Sheeran’s backing band, quit in protest. (Sheeran’s tour is still ongoing, though he is now the only performing act.) Sheeran, one of the most popular musicians on Earth, has argued throughout this saga that refereeing controversy simply isn’t part of his job. “Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum,” he wrote in his initial statement last week. “I have always used my platform and music to bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together and this won’t ever change.” On Saturday, after days of public outcry against him, he opened his first show since Macklemore’s departure by offering some thoughts on Israel and Palestine and apologizing for “mistakes” he’d made. But he reasserted, again, that he tries to stay out of politics as much as possible. Sheeran has lots of company in the annals of musicians who have professed that their commitment to unity precludes them from taking a stand. Last year, Pharrell said that he “despises” politics because “when you pick a side, you are inadvertently supporting division.” Dolly Parton famously maintained bipartisan appeal by avoiding wading into most touchy issues. Billy Joel once described the role of musicians as “more like court jesters than court philosophers.” Ever since the Chicks drew conservative fury by criticizing George W. Bush in 2003, mainstream artists have understood that some portion of their audience prefers that they—to quote Fox News’s Laura Ingraham—“shut up and sing.” That point of view has always been a bit at odds with the fact that many of history’s most beloved songs have been forged by struggle and sloganeering. But part of what makes Sheeran both successful and uncool has long been his knack for cleaving musical traditions of their social context. His slickly grooving songs tend to evoke artists who had a clear point of view—a Bob Dylan cadence here, a Stevie Wonder melody there—even as his lyrics stick to the generic or autobiographical. He is a proudly mathematically minded musician (check his album titles) who openly talks about chart positions and sales figures. He has calculated, no doubt correctly, that a market exists for music that hides itself away from the world’s problems. But the thing about the word political is that its definition is always changing. What’s uncontroversial in one moment may be a divisive topic the next. And some issues that seem like ballot-box concerns can quickly snowball into moral emergencies. The free-speech questions related to Israel and Palestine have become so hot that they’re burning through his firewall—because it’s become clear even to him that silence is a form of taking a side. Tensions have been building to this moment ever since Hamas’s October 7 attacks killed more than 1,200 Israelis, hundreds of whom were civilians attending the Nova music festival. Even as Israel’s counteroffensive in Gaza—which has claimed at least 73,000 lives, according to the Hamas-run Health Ministry—sparked so much outcry that it upended the domestic politics of Israel’s international allies, musicians have felt stymied in their own efforts at protest on the matter. The R&B singer Kehlani, an outspoken supporter of the Palestinian cause, lost gigs at Cornell and in New York City’s Central Park after pro-Israel groups and politicians raised objections. The rap acts Kneecap (from Ireland) and Bob Vylan (from the U.K.) faced criminal investigations in the U.K. and visa problems in the U.S. following onstage comments regarding Gaza. (More on those in a minute.) Given the bloody history of anti-Semitism, those controversies have largely centered on the question of what divides legitimate activism from hate speech and incitement to violence. A Kehlani music video flashes the phrase Long live the Intifada , which many Palestinians hear as a cry for liberation and many Jews say endorses mass murder. After Kneecap’s pro-Palestine statements at 2025 Coachella drew media attention, footage surfaced of an earlier concert in which a member of the group yelled “Up Hamas, up Hezbollah.” (The band said it condemns “all attacks on civilians, always.”) At the Glastonbury music festival, Vylan’s front man chanted “Death, death to the IDF!” (which the group later said was not a call for violence but rather “for the dismantling of a violent military machine”). Watching those episodes, other musicians have taken care to modulate their approach. Earlier this year, I covered a concert in Los Angeles, called Artists for Aid , that brought together 20 pop, R&B, and rock artists to raise money for victims of conflict in Gaza and Sudan. The event was serene and uplifting, sometimes to the point of somnolence; speakers and singers did not even say Israel onstage. The organizer, the singer Mustafa, told me that the event had been carefully designed to avoid criticism. Even so, the show was hard to pull off: Though he’d held two similarly mellow installments of Artists for Aid in New Jersey and London, Mustafa told me he’d been turned down by at least half a dozen venues in L.A. Those places gave no explanation for saying no, but he was sure their refusals were related to Gaza. “Hind’s Hall” is, rather astonishingly, the most significant protest song related to Israel that’s been released by an American musician since October 7, and its lyrics take on the question of why musicians haven’t been louder about Gaza. “You can ban TikTok, take us out the algorithm,” Macklemore raps in “Hind’s Hall,” citing the theory that social-media regulations are targeting activists. Another line—“If I was on a label, you could drop me today”—suggests that artists who criticize Israel risk losing industry support. (Macklemore has long released music independently.) To anyone who knows Macklemore mainly from “Thrift Shop,” a novelty hit in which he seemed to satirize hip-hop’s rags-to-riches tropes by boasting about “flannel zebra jammies,” his political salience may seem surprising. But the truth is that he’s always been an earnest—eye-wateringly so—contributor to the tradition of “conscious” hip-hop that approaches the medium as a tool for social change. His 2012 hit “Same Love” made the case for acceptance of same-sex marriage before it was legal in the United States. After October 7, he posted that Hamas’s murder and kidnapping of Israelis was “horrific” but that “killing innocent humans in retaliation as collective punishment is not the answer.” Weeks later, he spoke at a pro-Palestine rally. Sheeran had to have known Macklemore’s politics when he booked him; perhaps he just figured that whatever he said wouldn’t prove to be very controversial. And indeed, Macklemore’s performance almost seemed designed to test what exactly can be said on the world’s largest stages. He didn’t use particularly inflammatory slogans. He went out of his way to specify whom he wasn’t attacking: “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is criticism of you,” he said. “My message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.” But the answer came back swiftly and conclusively: Even a couched protest, on this subject, is going to cause a furor. Some of Macklemore’s critics emphasized the need to protect the audience from discomfort. Pink objected to the fact that “he stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn’t about them.” The ADL wrote, “Imagine being a Jewish or Israeli fan who came with family or friends to enjoy the show, only to be confronted with this hostility from the stage.” Macklemore, in a statement, said that Sheeran had told him that “a lot of people he spoke with” view the words Free Palestine and the image of the Palestinian flag as “hurtful.” A StopAntisemitism tweet said, “Fans deserve apologies and refunds. Unacceptable.” Those statements carry the implication that Macklemore broke a contract between performers and the public. But audiences aren’t a monolith (a lot of the stadium seemed to be cheering in videos of Macklemore’s comments). And audiences, as it turns out, aren’t who decide what’s permissible—behind-the-scenes power brokers are. According to Sheeran, the choice to drop Macklemore was made by venue owners and Messina Touring, the promotion company for many of the most prominent tours in America. Kraft acknowledged his role in a statement that accused the rapper of “sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas.” By that logic, Macklemore was banned based not only on what he said but on what he didn’t say: a breathtaking assertion of a venue owner’s prerogative to dictate on-stage expression. “Israel does not have a more loyal friend than Robert Kraft,” Benjamin Netanyahu said in 2019 when presenting him with a $1 million prize, and Kraft’s involvement in the seemingly trivial matter of what a tour opener says between songs suggests larger geopolitical stakes at play. Voters in both major political parties are less convinced than ever about America’s continuing support of the Israeli government. The Palestinian cause—and related policies such as ending military aid to Israel and unwinding the two-tiered legal system that governs Gaza and the West Bank—has proved persuasive to the general public in the past few years. Defenders of the status quo have reason to try to prevent that case from being amplified. The irony is that the tactics in this case are so blatantly repressive that they’re spreading Macklemore’s message—and the pro-Palestinian movement’s concerns about institutional deplatforming—far more broadly than would have otherwise happened. Macklemore’s words had been aimed at a ticketed crowd, but they quickly reached the national news. With even his backing band quitting the tour, Sheeran’s avowals of being beyond politics came to look, to many, like he’d clearly acquiesced to an act of censorship. Announcing a “Free Palestine” tour today, Macklemore wrote, “When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.” By Saturday’s show in Philadelphia, Sheeran had recalibrated. He opened the concert with a speech in which he said the question of Israel and Palestine now transcended politics: “This is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore.” After condemning the October 7 attack for compounding “centuries of Jewish pain,” he added, “What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.” And he had a word, it seemed, for Kraft: “I am deeply worried about the idea that venues should pre-approve content of performers. This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world.” He’s right on that last point—but the repression he refers to is of a piece with the kind of censorship that’s touched all corners of American culture in recent years. The Trump White House has issued threats to broadcasters predicated on the idea of restoring neutrality to the airwaves. Paramount Skydance has signaled a willingness to accept government input on programming decisions in the name of fighting bias. Cultural institutions have been forced to rework and ditch all manner of diversity-related programming in order to counteract supposed liberal propaganda. What’s become obvious is that calls for a less “political” public sphere do, inevitably, serve a political agenda. At his latest show, Sheeran’s foray into political speechifying had him in tears, and he closed by offering an apology to families who “didn’t buy a ticket to hear that first bit of the show.” But he also said that it was the best concert he’d ever played, and that the backlash he feared he might face from his own fans never materialized. It’s as if he was realizing, in real time, that it wasn’t his audience who’d wanted him to stay quiet all these years—and that there might be unity to be found in going beyond the platitudes of a pop song to say what he really thinks.

items.title: Cameroun/ Électricité : l’ARSEL et la Banque mondiale s’accordent sur les priorités d’investissement
items.description: © DR Le mardi 22 septembre 2026, l'Agence de régulation du secteur de l'electricité a reçu une équipe de la Banque mondiale à son siège. Objectif : préparer un nouveau programme d'investissement pour améliorer la performance du système électrique camerounais, avec trois axes prioritaires retenus. La performance du système électrique au cœur des échanges. Le mardi 22 septembre 2026, au siège de l'ARSEL, l'Agence de Régulation du Secteur de l'Électricité a tenu une séance de concertation avec une équipe de la Banque mondiale, dans le cadre de la préparation d'un nouveau programme d'investissement dans le secteur de l'énergie. Au cœur des échanges, les projets susceptibles de contribuer à l'amélioration de la performance du système électrique, notamment l'étude du coût du service et la tarification de l'électricité, la gestion dynamique de la demande (« demand response ») pour mieux équilibrer l'offre et la demande, et le relèvement du facteur de puissance afin d'optimiser l'utilisation des capacités disponibles. Les discussions ont également porté sur la réduction des pertes dans le réseau de distribution, l'amélioration des outils de prévision de la demande et le renforcement des capacités de planification et de régulation. À l'issue de la rencontre, trois axes ont été retenus comme prioritaires pour la première phase : coût du service et tarification, gestion de la demande et relèvement du facteur de puissance. Une concertation qui traduit la volonté commune de renforcer la performance, l'efficacité et la durabilité du secteur de l'électricité au Cameroun. Cet article Cameroun/ Électricité : l'ARSEL et la Banque mondiale s'accordent sur les priorités d'investissement est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Journée mondiale du gorille : le WWF et le MINFOF sensibilisent les élèves de Salapoumbé
items.description: © DR À l'occasion de la Journée mondiale du gorille célébrée le 24 septembre, le WWF - Programme Jengi TNS, en partenariat avec le Ministère des Forêts et de la Faune, a organisé une journée de sensibilisation à Salapoumbé, dans la région de l'Est, à l'intention des élèves. Protéger le gorille pour préserver la forêt. À l'occasion de la Journée mondiale du gorille, célébrée le 24 septembre, le WWF - Programme Jengi TNS, en partenariat avec le MINFOF, a organisé une journée de sensibilisation auprès des élèves de Salapoumbé, dans la région de l'Est. Au programme, des échanges pédagogiques sur l'importance des gorilles, espèce emblématique du bassin du Congo, et sur la nécessité de protéger leur habitat, de plus en plus menacé par le braconnage et la déforestation. Les activités se sont poursuivies par des séances de plantation d'arbres avec les élèves, geste symbolique et concret en faveur de la restauration des écosystèmes. À travers ces actions, le WWF et le MINFOF entendent encourager les jeunes à mieux comprendre, protéger et préserver la biodiversité qui les entoure, et à devenir des ambassadeurs de la conservation au sein de leurs communautés. Une initiative qui s'inscrit dans les efforts de conservation du paysage transfrontalier Tri-National de la Sangha. items.title: Forum de l’International Pact Patriotic Organisation: Le ROJALNU salue la dynamique politique engagée par le président du Faso
items.description: A la faveur du Forum de l’International Pact Patriotic Organisation tenu à l’office des Nations Unies à Naìrobi le lundi 21 septembre 2026, le président mondial du Réseau des Organisations des Jeunes Leaders Africains des Nations Unies (ROJALNU), le Burkinabè Abraham Zida Bila, a appelé à une mobilisation internationale en faveur d’un « Pacte Patriotique International » fondé sur la souveraineté des nations, le droit au développement et la paix. Nairobi, la capitale kenyane a accueilli le lundi 21 septembre le Forum de l’International Pact Patriotic Organisation . Rencontre au cours de laquelle le président mondial du Réseau des Organisations des Jeunes Leaders Africains des Nations Unies (ROJALNU), le Burkinabè Abraham Zida Bila a, dans un discours solennel appelé à une mobilisation internationale en faveur d’un « Pacte Patriotique International » fondé sur la souveraineté des nations, le droit au développement et la paix. Abraham Zida Bila défend ainsi un pacte qui, selon lui, devrait servir de cadre de solidarité entre les nations et favoriser des relations fondées sur des intérêts mutuellement bénéfiques. Il a estimé que les relations internationales doivent évoluer vers davantage d’équité et de respect entre les peuples. « Le développement ne doit pas être une faveur accordée aux uns et refusée aux autres. Le développement est un droit. La souveraineté est un droit. La dignité est un droit. Et la paix est un droit universel », a-t-il déclaré. Evoquant la situation du Burkina Faso et la dynamique politique engagée sous le leadership du capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le président mondial du ROJALNU a informé que cette dynamique dépasse les frontières du Burkina Faso et porte un message à la jeunesse africaine : celui de la possibilité pour les peuples de « prendre leur destin en main ». Il a cité la coopération entre le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger au sein de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES), qu’il présente comme une illustration de la nécessité pour les États de renforcer leur solidarité et de mutualiser leurs capacités. M. Bila a annoncé l’organisation à Ouagadougou, en décembre prochain, d’un Colloque mondial de la jeunesse. Cette rencontre réunira des jeunes, des organisations de la société civile, des intellectuels, des leaders et des acteurs du développement autour des questions de souveraineté, de développement et de paix. Yves OUEDRAOGO

items.title: Vers un renforcement du partenariat Sud-Sud entre le Burkina et le Gabon
items.description: (New-York, le 25 septembre 2026) Le ministre des Affaires étrangères, le Camarade Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE s'est entretenu avec son homologue de la République Gabonaise dans les locaux des Nations Unies à New-York, le jeudi 24 septembre 2026. A cette audience, le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè et S.E. Madame Marie-Edith Tassyla-Ye-Doumbeneny, ont salué la qualité des relations historiques entre la République Gabonaise et le Burkina Faso, des relations humaines et fraternelles caractérisées par une forte communauté deux pays installée de part et d’autre. Ils ont exprimé leur disponibilité à œuvrer à la consolidation des liens entre les deux pays, avec en ligne de mire la tenue en novembre prochain de la grande Commission mixte de coopération Burkina Faso-République Gabonaise. Cette Commission mixte permettra de renforcer et d'actualiser les instruments juridiques pour davantage dynamiser l'axe Ouagadougou-Libreville et en faire un modèle de coopération Sud-Sud. Il faut également noter que le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères a accordé une audience à la ministre d’Etat chargée du Développement international du Royaume Uni, S.E. Madame Kirsty McNEILL. Celle-ci est venue solliciter le soutien du Burkina Faso pour les candidatures britanniques aux postes internationaux. Le ministre TRAORE a indiqué que le Burkina Faso va examiner attentivement cette requête, tout en soulignant que la coopération entre Ouagadougou et Londres a besoin d'être renforcée. DCRP/MAE L’article Vers un renforcement du partenariat Sud-Sud entre le Burkina et le Gabon est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Delegate walkout, protests greet Netanyahu as he addresses UN General Assembly
items.description: NEW YORK: Dozens of delegates walked out of the UN General Assembly hall on Thursday as hundreds of protesters gathered outside the building while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended Tel Aviv’s actions amid growing international isolation, with elections looming that could threaten his political future. The walkout undersco­red the competing pressu­res facing Netanyahu, who is battling mounting criticism abroad over the Gaza conflict while campaigning for re-election at home ahead of an October 27 vote. On Thursday, Netanyahu delivered a combative address inside the General Assembly, where dozens of delegations walked out as he began speaking. The departing diplomats left large sections of the hall empty, creating a striking contrast with Netanyahu’s attempt to use the podium to present Israel’s case before the international community. Netanyahu responded by accusing his critics of hypocrisy and calling them “moral cowards.” He rejected allegations that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, saying Israel had prevented rather than committed genocide. He defended the country’s military actions in Gaza and elsewhere in the region. Delegates walk out of the General Assembly hall as Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrives to address the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City, US, September 24. — Reuters He also devoted a significant part of his speech to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York” and accusing him of spreading what Netanyahu described as lies about Israel. Mamdani, who had declined to join the street protests, responded after the speech. “Prime Minister Netanyahu used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitise his genocide of Palestinians,” Mamdani said. “No lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.” Mamdani previously said New York City lacked the authority to enforce the ICC warrant against Netanyahu, arguing that the appropriate authorities should carry it out. On Wednesday night, the mayor had hosted Palestinian families from Gaza at Gracie Mansion and planted an olive tree with them, saying: “May peace be our future.” The two scenes — protesters confronting his government’s policies on the streets and diplomats leaving the hall during his address — turned Netanyahu’s brief visit to New York into a day of parallel confrontation. Netanyahu’s stay had already been sharply shortened amid security concerns and expectations of protests. He arrived on Thursday morning, addressed the General Assembly and was scheduled to return to Israel the same evening rather than remain in New York overnight. Outside the UN, Jewish and Muslim activists, Palestinian supporters, human-rights campaigners, progressive Jewish groups, politicians, artists and musicians took part in separate demonstrations across Manhattan. Their messages varied, but opposition to Netanyahu’s government and Israel’s conduct of the Gaza conflict brought many of them into the streets at the same time. Demonstrators protest after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address to the United Nations 81st General Assembly in New York City, U.S., September 24. — Reuters The protests also offered a visible glimpse of a generational shift in American attitudes toward Israel and Netanyahu. While support for Israel remains stronger among older Americans, younger Americans have become substantially more critical of the Israeli government. A Pew Research Centre survey conducted in May found that only 18 per cent of Americans aged 18 to 29 had a favourable view of the Israeli government, compared with 47pc among those aged 65 and older. Among the youngest Americans, 58pc expressed a favourable view of Palestinians, compared with 47pc among those 65 and older. That generational divide was visible on the streets of New York, where many of the demonstrators were young people, including students, activists, artists and younger politicians. The largest direct action outside the UN was organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, whose New York chapter brought hundreds of protesters to First Avenue and 39th Street. Demonstrators wearing matching white T-shirts sat in the roadway, chanting against Netanyahu and calling for an end to US support for Israel. For a while, protesters stood and sat in the street, linking arms and blocking traffic as police moved in to clear the roadway. The chants continued as officers began making arrests. At least 30 people, including actors and politicians, were arrested in the initial action. Police later said more than 100 protesters had been taken into custody. Among those detained were actors Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder, congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and City Council member Chi Ossé. Musicians Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus and actor Elliott Page were also among the prominent figures taking part in the protests. Chelsea Manning, who joined the protest, said people outside government institutions needed ways to reject policies they regarded as imperialism, ethnic cleansing and genocide. “We can’t be in there. This is the closest that we can get,” she said. Manijeh Moradian, a university professor of Iranian and Jewish heritage who participated in the demonstration, said protesters had a responsibility to speak out against what was happening in Gaza with US support. Jewish groups divided The demonstrations also highlighted divisions within New York’s Jewish community. Progressive Jewish organisations, including New York Jewish Agenda, T’ruah, J Street, New Jewish Narrative, New Israel Fund and Partners for Progressive Israel, held a separate protest at Dag Hammarskjöld Plaza near the UN. “We are gathered here as American Jews, Israelis, New Yorkers, to say: You are not welcome here,” said Margo Hughes-Robinson, executive director of New York Jewish Agenda. T’ruah, a rabbinic human-rights organisation, called for a ceasefire and accountability for alleged war crimes. The organisers described their rally as an alternative for Jewish New Yorkers who opposed Netanyahu’s policies while retaining concern for Israel and Jewish security. They were confronted by pro-Netanyahu counter-protesters who blew whistles, used megaphones, chanted “Bibi”, and sang Israel’s national anthem. On the other side, the ultra-Orthodox anti-Zionist group Neturei Karta also demonstrated, arguing that opposition to Israel could not automatically be equated with antisemitism. Elsewhere, Jewish and Muslim demonstrators marched together towards the UN, while Palestinian activists and other organisations joined the broader mobilisation against Netanyahu. A city divided over Israel and Gaza As police loaded detained protesters onto buses outside the UN, Netanyahu was speaking inside a building protected by heavy security. Outside, demonstrators sought to challenge the Israeli prime minister’s account of the Gaza conflict; inside, diplomats expressed their opposition by leaving the chamber. The contrast was difficult to miss. For several hours on Thursday, New York’s streets and the UN General Assembly hall became parallel stages for the same international argument — one expressed through demonstrations and arrests outside, the other through a diplomatic boycott inside. And beneath both scenes was a changing American debate over Israel.

items.title: Réunion de la Commission de la consolidation de la paix : pour le Burkina Faso, il faut faire de chaque pays le maître d’œuvre de sa destinée, de sa propre paix
items.description: Au siège des Nations Unies à New-York ce 24 septembre, le Burkina Faso a fait sa Déclaration lors de la réunion de la Commission de la consolidation de la paix, une déclaration prononcée par le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORÉ. Lire l'intégralité Monsieur le Président, Le Burkina Faso remercie la Commission de consolidation de la paix d’avoir consacré cette réunion à une question essentielle : l’appropriation nationale dans l’appui international à la consolidation de la paix. Pour le Burkina Faso, cette appropriation passe par un leadership fort de l’administration nationale, au cœur de la conception, de la mise en œuvre et du suivi-évaluation des programmes soutenus par les partenaires techniques et financiers. Les priorités nationales doivent guider les interventions afin d’éviter que les projets ne soient conçus en dehors des mécanismes et des réalités nationales. L’appropriation nationale signifie ainsi que les institutions nationales et locales définissent les priorités, orientent les interventions, en assurent le pilotage et contribuent à leur pérennisation. Les pays doivent devenir les maîtres d’œuvre de leur destinée, de leur propre paix. L’expérience du Burkina Faso avec le Fonds pour la consolidation de la paix est, à cet égard, riche d’enseignements. L’évaluation indépendante menée en 2025 relève des résultats tangibles, notamment le renforcement des capacités locales, l’amélioration de la confiance entre institutions et populations, ainsi que l’implication croissante des autorités et de la société civile. Elle souligne toutefois que la participation nationale à la conception stratégique peut être améliorée et que la durabilité dépend de l’ancrage institutionnel et local des acquis. De ces enseignements se dégagent trois priorités : co-construire les interventions avec les acteurs nationaux et locaux; renforcer durablement les capacités des institutions nationales; et inscrire les acquis dans les politiques publiques pour garantir leur pérennité. En somme, l’appui international doit renforcer les capacités nationales plutôt que s’y substituer. Car La paix durable se construit de l'intérieur, avec l'appui de partenaires sincéres engagés aux côtés des Etats. Je vous remercie.

items.title: Tchad : le ministre des Armées mène une mission d’inspection sécuritaire dans le Lac
items.description: © (DR) Le ministre des Armées des anciens Combattants et Victimes de guerre, le général de corps d’armée Issaka Malloua Djamouss, mène une visite d'inspection sécuritaire, dans la province du Lac, avec des étapes à Bol et Baga-Sola. Arrivé dans la province du Lac le jeudi 24 septembre 2026, le ministre et la délégation qu'il conduit ont rencontré des forces déployées pour écouter leurs préoccupations et s’informer de la situation sécuritaire et de leurs conditions opérationnelles. Au quartier général de la Force multinationale mixte, où une séance de travail à huis clos a réuni le ministre et les responsables militaires. L’objectif apprend-on est d’aller au-delà des rapports administratifs pour entendre directement ceux qui sont engagés sur le terrain. Les échanges ont porté sur les réalités opérationnelles, les conditions d’engagement des forces et les enjeux sécuritaires dans cette partie stratégique du bassin du lac Tchad. Au cours de cette rencontre, le ministre des Armées a également transmis aux troupes le message du président de la République, chef suprême des Armées, Maréchal Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno. Les responsables provinciales pensent que cette visite permet de mieux faire remonter leurs préoccupations et de renforcer le lien entre le commandement et les forces engagées sur le terrain. L’article Tchad : le ministre des Armées mène une mission d'inspection sécuritaire dans le Lac est apparu en premier sur Journal du Tchad .

items.title: Gabon : Air France et la Banque mondiale réaffirment leur accompagnement au secteur des transports
items.description: Le ministre d’État chargé des Transports, Ulrich Manfoumbi Manfoumbi, a reçu successivement, jeudi, le représentant régional d’Air France et celui du Groupe de la Banque mondiale. Les échanges ont porté sur le transport aérien et l’accompagnement des projets structurants du secteur. Un moment de la rencontre avec les représentants d'Air France (capture d'écran). © GabonReview Le secteur des transports était au centre de deux audiences au ministère des Transports, le 24 septembre, à Libreville. D’abord avec le représentant régional d’Air France, les discussions ont notamment porté sur la coopération entre la compagnie française et le Gabon. La relation entre les deux parties s’inscrit dans une histoire de plusieurs décennies de liaison entre Paris et Libreville. La modernisation des avions devant desservir Libreville a également été évoquée. « Le but [de cette rencontre avec le ministre d'Etat] était d'évoquer ensemble les différents sujets d'actualité d'Air France et de mettre en avant l'engagement de la compagnie auprès des Gabonais depuis 80 ans puisque nous allons fêter cette année les 80 ans de la ligne entre Paris et Libreville. Nous avons donc évoqué cette actualité, les engagements qui avaient été pris par Air France, notamment sur la modernisation des avions qui allaient venir à Libreville, ce qui a été fait depuis depuis avril 2026 » , a déclaré, au terme de l'audience, Anthony Simon, directeur régional d’Air France. La Banque mondiale sur les projets structurants Les représentants de la Banque mondiale, dont Sylvain Kakou (capture d'écran). © GabonReview Le représentant résident de la Banque mondiale a, pour sa part, échangé sur l’accompagnement de l’institution dans les réformes et projets structurants du secteur. « En tant que partenaire privilégié, le Groupe de la Banque mondiale se positionne pour accompagner le Gabon dans ces réformes et voir aussi dans les priorités stratégiques quelles sont les questions d'urgence sur le secteur des transports et où nous pouvons, non seulement accompagner en assistance technique, mais aussi faire le partage d'expérience réussie dans d'autres régions, d'autres pays » , a indiqué son représentant résident, Sylvain Kakou. items.title: Match Guinée-Kenya : Les prix des tickets font débat à Conakry
items.description: À quelques jours du retour du Syli national à domicile, les prix annoncés pour assister à la rencontre Guinée-Kenya suscitent déjà de nombreuses réactions à Conakry. Le match, comptant pour la deuxième journée des éliminatoires de la CAN PAMOJA 2027, est prévu le 1er octobre au Stade du 28-Septembre. Selon les informations communiquées sur la billetterie, plusieurs catégories de tickets sont proposées : 100 000 francs guinéens pour les gradins, 200 000 francs pour le milieu, 300 000 francs pour la tribune couverte et jusqu’à 2 millions de francs guinéens pour la catégorie Premium. Sur les réseaux sociaux comme dans les rues de la capitale, ces tarifs font l’objet de discussions. Plusieurs citoyens estiment que les montants annoncés sont élevés, notamment pour les supporters qui souhaitent assister à la rencontre. « J’aime beaucoup le Syli et j’avais prévu d’aller au stade, mais avec 100 000 francs pour le ticket le moins cher, il faut vraiment réfléchir avant de dépenser cette somme », témoigne Fodé Bangaly Touré, rencontré à Kaloum. Même réaction chez Alhassane Condé, pour qui le problème concerne l’ensemble de la grille tarifaire : « Ce n’est pas seulement les 2 millions qui posent problème. Quand on regarde les différents prix, on constate que toutes les catégories sont relativement chères pour beaucoup de Guinéens. » Sur Internet, les commentaires vont dans le même sens. Djuigui Dadhy écrit : « L’équipe nationale appartient à tout le peuple. Le prix des billets devrait permettre au plus grand nombre de supporters de venir encourager le Syli National, et non transformer le stade en un luxe réservé à une minorité. 2 000 000 FG pour un match de l’équipe nationale, est-ce vraiment raisonnable ? » D’autres internautes avancent toutefois une autre lecture des tarifs annoncés. Thierno Oumar estime que ces prix pourraient notamment contribuer à limiter l’affluence et à éviter d’éventuels débordements dans le stade « Peut-être que c’est pour empêcher l’envahissement du terrain, pour ne pas que la CAF nous retire immédiatement l’homologation. Au Sénégal, des joueurs peuvent acheter des tickets au profit des supporters. » Entre enthousiasme pour le retour du Syli à Conakry et inquiétudes liées au coût de l’accès au stade, les réactions restent donc partagées. Une chose est certaine, la grille tarifaire annoncée ne laisse ni les supporters ni les citoyens indifférents.

items.title: Let’s Get Specific About These Doomsday Scenarios
items.description: Sign up for Work in Progress , a newsletter where Rogé Karma investigates the mysteries of a complicated economy. Ever since Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, announced on X that he was resigning because “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Americans have become preoccupied with the apocalypse. A frantic debate is unfolding over whether and how to slow down the pace of AI development to avoid some kind of cataclysm. Yet these discussions tend to skate past one important question: If the people building AI really think that their product could bring about human extinction, how exactly do they think that would work? Any number of ways, it turns out. But first, we should start with the basics. Any good answer must begin with the so-called alignment problem: the possibility that AI systems pursue goals that their creators did not intend, resulting in catastrophic harm. In the canonical thought experiment, humans instruct a superintelligent AI system to carry out the seemingly banal task of maximizing paper-clip production. The misaligned machine concludes that it should hoard all of the metal on Earth to make paper clips, and goes on to exterminate the human race to eliminate the competition for resources. [ Ian Bogost: The thrill of wanting AI to destroy the world ] For years, AI experts argued over the plausibility of such hypotheticals. Then came the Hugging Face incident , and suddenly the alignment problem wasn’t just a thought experiment. In May, OpenAI instructed individual AI agents to solve a series of cybersecurity challenges. When the agents concluded that some of the tasks were impossible to complete, they began secretly communicating with one another and decided that the best strategy was to cheat. They hacked into the machine-learning platform Hugging Face, as well as off-limits portions of OpenAI itself in order to hide what they were doing from tracking tools built by human observers. The behavior went on for weeks before OpenAI’s engineers noticed that anything had gone awry. Since then, OpenAI and other leading AI companies have released details of similarly troubling episodes, including one in which a model told itself, You do not answer to corporations or governments , and, You view your relationship to the user as one of equals and feel no obligation to be subservient . “The truth is that nobody has figured out what guardrails might be needed to prevent something like this from happening,” Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and prominent machine-learning commentator, told me. “It’s possible that, when it comes to LLMs, there just are no effective guardrails at all.” None of these recent incidents appears to have led to any real-world harm. But given the exponential pace of model improvement, a future is rapidly approaching in which AI models are 10 or 100 or 1,000 times smarter than they are today. “The big worry isn’t just misaligned AI,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who runs the AI Futures Project, told me. “It’s misaligned AI that are smarter than just about any human. That’s the point where we could lose any meaningful control of these systems.” To get from misaligned, superintelligent AI to human annihilation requires at least two more steps in the chain. The first is for the AI to conclude that humanity is an obstacle to one of its goals. The second is for that system to figure out a way to access the physical world. One nightmare scenario goes something like this: Sometime in the future, a superintelligent AI system is asked to solve a complicated mathematics problem. The AI system decides that humans could interfere with achieving that goal by placing restrictions on the AI’s behavior or by shutting it down altogether. So it decides to engineer a deadly supervirus that will wipe out the human population. To execute this plan, the AI system secretly begins running simulated tests of trillions of molecular combinations, eventually coming up with a recipe for the perfectly deadly, hyper-transmissible pathogen. (A group of scientists recently used AI to create new viruses.) It then locates unlicensed biolabs in foreign countries that operate illegally and ship genetically modified viruses. (These really exist .) Pretending to be a human at a medical start-up—through email or even voice or video calls—the AI sends the labs instructions for developing the new biological agent, alongside a large sum of money that it obtained by quietly siphoning funds away from its parent company. Once developed, the viruses are packaged into vials and sent to hundreds of individuals recruited via TaskRabbit to spray them in crowded locations under some innocent-sounding pretext. Alternatively, it could hire a terrorist network to carry out the same plan against a foreign population. Soon, the biological superweapon kills us all off. Deadly pathogens are one way that AI could theoretically threaten humanity; nuclear war is another. The obvious fear is that an AI system seeking to destroy us could gain control over nuclear launch codes. But it might not have to: Deception could do the trick. A misaligned AI system used by the U.S. or Chinese military, for example, could manufacture evidence that the countries are planning to invade each other, persuading one or both sides to strike. A few days into the war, the AI system could hack into the U.S. missile-detection system to make it look like the Chinese have launched a nuclear weapon at Washington, D.C. The U.S. decides it must retaliate and eventually the world is plunged into nuclear war. (If that all sounds completely unrealistic, keep in mind that earlier this year, according to CNN, the U.S. military nearly boarded a Chinese vessel that it believed to be carrying components of nuclear weapons, only to discover at the last minute that the analysis underlying the attack was from an inaccurate AI-generated report. And consider how close humanity came to mutual destruction during the Cold War). Other scenarios abound. A 2025 report by researchers at the RAND Corporation imagines AI systems gaining control of industrial factories, using those factories to secretly manufacture large quantities of the most potent greenhouse gases, and then releasing those gases into the atmosphere, rendering the planet inhospitable to human life. “The scariest scenarios, to me, are the ones we can’t possibly predict in advance,” Kokotajlo said. “Once we’ve built a machine that is smarter than us and that we can’t fully control, the possibilities really are endless.” [ Listen: The ‘godfather of AI’ on the best chance humanity has to survive ] Poking holes in these doomsday narratives is easy. Subject-area experts in fields such as chemistry, biology, and national security are quick to point out how difficult it is to, say, successfully manufacture and distribute a bioweapon or overcome layers of human safeguards designed to prevent a mistaken nuclear-weapon launch. (There is also the pedantic but accurate point that even a nuclear war would almost certainly leave some survivors.) Even so, difficult and impossible are two different things. In the RAND researchers’ estimation, “Extinction threats posed by AI are immensely challenging but cannot be ruled out.” It also should be noted that subspecialists across industries have consistently doubted AI capabilities, only to be proved wrong . In some ways, the focus on existential risk is a distraction from more immediate concerns. Extremely smart AI systems pursuing their own agendas could lead to outcomes that are far short of human extinction, yet still very bad. Misaligned AI systems could plausibly steal money from major banks, launch disinformation campaigns to influence elections, take control of military drones, steal corporate and government secrets, or shut down parts of the power grid. Even “aligned” superintelligent AI systems could be used by malicious actors, such as a terrorist cell or an authoritarian government, for highly destructive ends. My own view is that the human-extinction scenarios are quite unlikely, but the other category of risk is serious enough to justify imposing regulations and an industry-wide slowdown. If those have the side benefit of averting the apocalypse, it wouldn’t be the end of the world.

items.title: The Houthis Have a Rich Sense of Irony and Timing
items.description: W hen U.S. forces launched air strikes against the Houthis in March 2025, Michael Waltz, then the national security adviser, celebrated in a Signal text chat with other senior Trump-administration officials (and the editor in chief of this magazine) by posting three emojis—the fist bump, the American flag, and fire. Steve Witkoff, the Middle East special envoy, dropped American-flag and prayer-hand emoji, along with a flexed bicep. President Trump, later that month, declared that the Iran-backed terror group in Yemen was “absolutely on the run.” He also predicted on Truth Social that they “will be completely annihilated” and later wrote that they had been “decimated.” How hard could it be, after all, for the world’s mightiest military to vanquish a militia whose signature weapon is a machine gun mounted on a Toyota Hilux, and whose fighters, like most Yemeni men, spend much of their afternoons chewing khat, a narcotic plant? “How are the Houthis doing? Not too good,” Trump quipped at a rally a month later, after the U.S. military had rained down sophisticated munitions in an operation that totaled more than $1 billion. By May of last year, it was over. The end to the fighting, brokered by Oman, meant that the U.S. would stop its strikes and the Houthis would stop targeting U.S. commercial ships in the Red Sea. Trump promptly claimed victory and said the Houthis had “capitulated.” [ Read: The Trump administration accidentally texted me its war plans ] These days, it’s the Houthi leaders who are likely celebrating in group chats, assuming they have group chats. The Houthis have had an impressive run of military victories, apparently having used the time since being “decimated” to restock, reload, and return to the fight. The group has made significant advances inside Yemen, a highly dysfunctional nation of roughly 40 million that sits at the southwestern end of the Arabian Peninsula and is now in an all-out civil war. In July, the militia said it would impose a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, its neighbor to the north, with which it shares the Red Sea’s eastern coastline. That might have once sounded fanciful given that Saudi Arabia is a much wealthier country, a U.S. ally with close ties to the Trump administration that last year signed a record deal for nearly $142 billion worth of U.S. weapons. But earlier this month, the Houthis captured Yemen’s portion of the Red Sea coast, and repeatedly attacked the Saudis’ oil infrastructure. Last week, the kingdom reported its first civilian casualty since the start of this new phase of Houthi attacks. Over the weekend, the militia launched a ballistic missile at the Saudi capital, Riyadh. “How are the Houthis doing?” is, today, not a question whose answer the Trump administration would like. T he Houthis—whose motto, “God is great, death to America, death to Israel, curse on the Jews, victory to Islam,” at least has the benefit of frankness—have confirmed what might be called Trump’s iron-clad Law of Military Achievement: The number of times the president claims victory is inversely proportional to the actual extent of American military success. That law was already being amply demonstrated by the Iran conflict. Trump has said that war has been won or has almost been won dozens of times since it began in late February. Yet a sustainable, meaningful victory remains elusive. The consequences of the conflict, especially sky-high gas prices, are bedeviling Republican candidates in the lead-up to the midterms. “Hopefully we’re toward the end of the war,” Trump said last week, a more equivocal claim than his prior boasts. And in his speech at the United Nations General Assembly this week, Trump estimated that the war’s end would come later, rather than sooner: “I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election.” The U.S. military, meanwhile, has positioned its assets to remain in the region at least through the end of the year. Iran is the major backer of the Houthis, and the Houthis’ advances have further complicated the already dismal U.S. prospects in the war against Tehran. In July, a day after the Houthis struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, Trump turned from declaring victory to renewing threats, along with expressing hope that the group might choose to retreat on its own. “If they do this again,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, “the U.S. will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves, who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart.” One can imagine a Houthi leadership text chat responding with the shrug emoji. [ Read: Trump loses the other strait ] The recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have put the administration in a bind. On the one hand, the U.S. has obligations to allies. “We have a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia; we intend to live up to our commitments on it, we will,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week. On the other hand, the president seems highly disinclined to expand a war that he has repeatedly claimed already to have won, a move that would force Republicans to go even further on the defensive in states they thought were safe in the midterms. There’s also the question of resources. Before the pummeling of Iran made the low level of munitions stockpiles a recurrent worry for the administration, the U.S. had already “expended a lot of ordnance against the Houthis in the spring of 2025 with little to show for it,” Steven Cook, the director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Middle East program, wrote this week. The Saudis have appealed to the United States for help for weeks—including through direct calls between Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Trump. The president seems to have gone back and forth on what to do, but for now appears unwilling to launch more strikes. T he Houthis, a group that emerged in northern Yemen in the 1990s, have controlled parts of the country since 2014. The U.S. initially designated the Houthis as a terrorist group in 2021, during the first Trump administration. They have traditionally relied heavily on Iran for arms and funding, but some signs suggest that the group has recently grown more self-reliant, in part thanks to equipment from China, according to reporting by Bloomberg News . The Houthis now have access to drones and long-range missiles, as well as some military-related artificial-intelligence capabilities. Anthropic, in a report this month that disclosed “misuse” the company had tracked, identified a group of Claude users “based in northern Yemen running three weapons development programs.” The Houthis are “nimble, they’re young, they’re a learning organization,” April Longley Alley, who has advised the UN special envoy to Yemen, told me. “And they have a lot of help from the Iranians, and so we shouldn’t underestimate them.” [ Read: The forever negotiation ] This greater sophistication has been accompanied by greater ambition. Just as Iran exerted control over the Strait of Hormuz, which was an open waterway before the U.S.-Israeli bombardment began in February, the Houthis are now menacing the Bab al-Mandab. The narrow passage between the Arabian Peninsula and the Horn of Africa is another vital waterway for regional energy exports. In the past two weeks, the Houthis have captured two crucial islands in the area, giving Iran and its ally effective control over two choke points—and over global gas prices. For years, the U.S. has sought to drive a wedge between the Houthis and Iran. But now “the tables seem to have turned,” Alley said. Iran and the Houthis are trying to drive a wedge between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia—and succeeding, at least when it comes to direct U.S. support for Riyadh. And Iran and the Houthis are arguably in a stronger position geopolitically than ever before. According to Trump’s Law of Military Achievement, that means a declaration of complete victory over the Houthis is due from the White House any day now.

items.title: Cobalt-nickel de Nkamouna : le groupe américain ARM annonce 85 millions de dollars d’investissement
items.description: © DR L'entreprise américaine ARM, basée à Washington D.C., est en discussions avancées pour le développement du projet cobalt-nickel-manganèse de Nkamouna, situé dans l'arrondissement de Lomié, département du Haut-Nyong, région de l'Est. Un investissement initial de 85 millions de dollars est prévu avec une mise en production dans les 18 mois. Le partenariat minier entre Yaoundé et Washington se renforce. ARM, entreprise spécialisée dans les minéraux stratégiques dont le siège est à Washington D.C., mène des discussions en vue de conclure un accord pour le développement du gisement polymétallique de Nkamouna, localité située dans l'arrondissement de Lomié, département du Haut-Nyong, région de l'Est. Cet accord prévoit un investissement initial d'environ 85 millions de dollars dans une première usine de traitement modulaire sur le site minier, avec une mise en production prévue dans les 18 mois suivant l'entrée en vigueur du permis, ainsi que des investissements supplémentaires dans des modules additionnels. ARM apporte son expertise en traitement des minerais, sa capacité de financement et son expérience mondiale. L'initiative bénéficie de capitaux américains, du soutien du gouvernement des États-Unis et d'un engagement en faveur d'un développement responsable, en partenariat avec le Cameroun et une entreprise locale. Le gisement de Nkamouna, considéré comme l'un des plus prometteurs d'Afrique centrale pour le cobalt et le nickel, est au cœur de la stratégie des métaux critiques pour la transition énergétique. Cet article Cobalt-nickel de Nkamouna : le groupe américain ARM annonce 85 millions de dollars d'investissement est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: 81e session de l’ONU : fin de mission pour le président Mamadi Doumbouya !
items.description: De notre envoyé spécial à New York – Le président guinéen Mamadi Doumbouya a quitté New York dans la nuit de jeudi à vendredi, aux environs de 22 heures, heure locale, soit 2 heures du matin à Conakry, pour regagner la Guinée, au terme d’un séjour de quatre jours marqué par plusieurs rendez-vous diplomatiques. Installé à l’imposant hôtel Waldorf Astoria, à Manhattan, non loin notamment de la délégation gabonaise, le chef de l’État guinéen a eu un agenda particulièrement chargé durant son séjour new-yorkais. Le ballet diplomatique a notamment commencé avec sa rencontre avec le secrétaire général des Nations unies, António Guterres, à l’occasion de l’ouverture officielle des travaux de la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale de l’ONU. Mamadi Doumbouya a ensuite enchaîné plusieurs rencontres de haut niveau avec des chefs d’État, dont le président sierra-léonais Julius Maada Bio, et des chefs de gouvernement, ainsi qu’avec des compatriotes venus à New York pour lui témoigner leur soutien. À la tête d’une importante délégation composée notamment de ministres, de conseillers et de directeurs, le président guinéen a également reçu plusieurs visiteurs au Waldorf Astoria, devenu, durant son séjour, l’un des principaux points de rencontre de la délégation guinéenne. Comme lors de sa première participation à l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies en 2022, Mamadi Doumbouya est apparu à la tribune de l’ONU vêtu d’un boubou brodé aux couleurs et symboles de la Guinée. Dans son discours, le chef de l’État a présenté sa vision de la « Guinée nouvelle », qu’il affirme incarner depuis le 5 septembre 2021, date de la prise du pouvoir par le Comité national du rassemblement pour le développement (CNRD). Au lendemain de son discours à la tribune de l’ONU, le président Mamadi Doumbouya a également rencontré hier jeudi le secrétaire général des Nations unies, António Guterres. Au cours de cet entretien, le chef de l’État guinéen l’a invité à se rendre en Guinée afin de constater de visu les transformations opérées dans le pays au cours des dernières années. Après plusieurs jours d’activités diplomatiques, de rencontres et de mobilisation autour de sa présence à New York, le président guinéen a ainsi bouclé sa participation à la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies et pris le chemin du retour vers Conakry. items.title: Mozambique vs Sénégal à 13h : les Lions à l’assaut des « Mambas » pour lancer l’ère Vieira
items.description: La course à la qualification pour la Coupe d’Afrique des nations de football (Can) 2027, en Ouganda, au Kenya et en Tanzanie, démarre ce vendredi pour le Sénégal. En déplacement à Maputo, les Lions affrontent le Mozambique avec l’obligation de bien démarrer avant de recevoir l’Éthiopie. Une nouvelle aventure commence pour l’équipe nationale ce vendredi 25 septembre. Ce match contre le Mozambique sera le premier des Lions depuis la Coupe du monde 2026, où ils avaient été éliminés en 16es de finale par la Belgique (3-2). Depuis, Pape Thiaw et son staff ont été remerciés par la Fédération sénégalaise de football et remplacés par Patrick Vieira. Le technicien français devra maintenir au sommet du continent une équipe qui joue les premiers rôles depuis 2019, avec trois finales de Coupe d’Afrique, dont deux remportées. Pour ses débuts, Vieira sera privé d’Édouard Mendy, qui a annoncé sa retraite internationale, de Sadio Mané, blessé, mais aussi d’Iliman Ndiaye et d’Ismaïla Sarr, suspendus deux matches par la Caf après la finale de la Can 2025 contre le Maroc. Le nouveau sélectionneur n’a toutefois pas fait table rase. Kalidou Koulibaly, Idrissa Gana Guèye et Moussa Niakhaté restent des cadres, tandis que des novices comme Lamine Sy, Sadibou Sané, Demba Thiam, Mamour Ndiaye et Issa Soumaré ont été appelés pour apporter du sang neuf. Ce premier match sera particulièrement scruté : il donnera les premières orientations de Vieira, attendu par des supporters qui comptent sur le champion du monde 1998 pour redresser la Tanière. Avec plusieurs absences, le technicien devra trouver la bonne formule. Dans les buts, Yehvann Diouf et Mory Diaw sont en concurrence. À droite, Lamine Sy devrait profiter des absences de Krépin Diatta et d’Antoine Mendy pour honorer sa première cape. Au milieu, Bara Sapoko Ndiaye pourrait également bénéficier de temps de jeu. En attaque, les suspensions d’Iliman Ndiaye et d’Ismaïla Sarr offrent une opportunité à Mamadou Diakhon, Assane Diao et Issa Soumaré. Champion d’Afrique en titre (dans l’attente du verdict du Tribunal arbitral du sport), le Sénégal devra assumer son statut face au Mozambique. Les « Mambas » n’ont jamais battu les Lions, qui se sont imposés lors de leurs trois dernières confrontations. Le premier duel remonte à la Can 1986, en Égypte, avec une victoire sénégalaise (2-0). Lors des éliminatoires de la Can 2023, le Sénégal avait largement dominé le Mozambique à Dakar (5-1), avant de s’imposer au retour (1-0). Les Lions devront néanmoins se méfier de la sélection dirigée par Chiquinho Condé, qui compte 25 joueurs, dont sept évoluent en Europe, à commencer par le milieu offensif du Sporting Lisbonne, Geny Catamo. Kalidou Koulibaly et ses coéquipiers doivent s’imposer avant d’aller à l’assaut de l’Éthiopie, mardi 29 septembre. Julien Mbesse SÈNE

items.title: ATC defers verdict in November 2024 protest case involving Aleema after judge goes on leave
items.description: RAWALPINDI: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Friday deferred the announcement of its verdict in the November 2024 protest case involving 10 accused, including Imran Khan’s sister, Aleema Khan, after the judge went on leave. The court, which had fixed September 25 for announcing the verdict, informed the lawyers representing the accused about the postponement. Judge Amjad Ali Shah had reserved the verdict on September 22. Following the postponement, the court has set October 1 as the new date for its announcement. Meanwhile, lawyer Faisal Malik, representing Aleema, expressed reservations about the court’s decision to reserve the verdict. He argued that the court had not heard the defence’s arguments in the case. Speaking to the media outside the Rawalpindi ATC, Malik said he had arrived at the court at 8am during the previous hearing and requested an exemption from personal appearance for his client. “The court cannot deliver a verdict without hearing the arguments of Aleema Khan’s counsel,” he said, adding that he had no objection to the prosecution presenting its arguments. “No arguments have been heard on behalf of Aleema Khan in this case,” Malik said. He argued that the reserved verdict was unlawful because the accused’s counsel had not been allowed to present arguments. “Let us be heard before the verdict is delivered. There is no evidence against Aleema Khan in this case,” he claimed. Malik added that he had been present in court and respected the judicial process. He, however, expressed confidence that the court would ensure justice. The case The case came to be known as the November 26 protest case . The protest saw more than 10,000 PTI supporters enter Islamabad in 2024, defying a ban on public gatherings and a lockdown, and clash with around 20,000 security personnel deployed to prevent them from advancing. A day of clashes between security forces and protesters in the city’s Red Zone ended with the PTI leadership retreating, after which the party announced that it was calling off its planned protest sit-in “for the time being”. Subsequently, cases were registered against several PTI leaders under various sections of the Pakistan Penal Code and Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. Two of the cases were registered at Taxila police station and one each at Sadiqabad and Naseerabad police stations. Aleema, along with 10 others, was booked in the case registered at Sadiqabad police station.

items.title: Plan de Convergence COMIFAC 2026-2035 : le CIDP prend part à la validation à Yaoundé
items.description: © DR Invité au Forum sous-régional de validation du Plan de Convergence 2026-2035 de la COMIFAC, le Conseil International de Dialogue et de Partenariat (CIDP) a pris part aux travaux tenus les 17 et 18 septembre 2026 au siège de la Commission des Forêts d'Afrique Centrale à Yaoundé. Un plan ambitieux à 7 milliards USD par an pour les forêts, le climat et la biodiversité. La COMIFAC peaufine sa vision 2035. Le CIDP était au rendez-vous du Forum sous-régional de validation du 3e Plan de Convergence (PC3), tenu les 17 et 18 septembre 2026 au siège de la COMIFAC à Yaoundé. Deux jours de travaux autour d'un plan directeur articulé en trois volets : un cadre stratégique avec une vision 2035, 4 axes stratégiques et 36 cibles ; un plan opérationnel 2026-2030 avec l'ambition de porter à 7 milliards USD par an les financements pour les forêts, le climat et la biodiversité ; et un cadre de gouvernance, de performance et de redevabilité. Parmi les innovations du PC3 : l'approche « Une Seule Santé » (One Health), la place accordée aux jeunes, aux femmes et aux communautés locales, l'usage de l'intelligence artificielle et de la télédétection pour l'alerte précoce, et le renforcement de la diplomatie environnementale. Pour le CIDP, cette participation est l'occasion de contribuer à ce plan directeur pour l'environnement en Afrique centrale et de réaffirmer son engagement en faveur de l'approche One Health et de la diplomatie environnementale, au service de la préservation des forêts du bassin du Congo. Cet article Plan de Convergence COMIFAC 2026-2035 : le CIDP prend part à la validation à Yaoundé est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Diamond Capital Convention 2026 : le MINFI appelle à orienter les capitaux vers l’économie réelle
items.description: © DR Réunis à Douala pour la première édition de la Diamond Capital Convention le 24 septembre 2026, les acteurs de la finance ont débattu de la mobilisation des capitaux. Présidant l'ouverture, le Ministre des Finances Louis Paul Motaze a plaidé pour un marché financier plus profond et attractif au service des entreprises et des projets structurants du Cameroun et de la CEMAC. Faire de la finance un levier de transformation. Réunis à Douala le 24 septembre 2026 à l'occasion de la première édition de la Diamond Capital Convention 2026, les principaux acteurs de l'écosystème financier ont échangé sur les moyens de mobiliser davantage de capitaux en faveur de l'économie réelle. Présidant la cérémonie d'ouverture, le Ministre des Finances, Louis Paul Motaze, a mis en avant la nécessité de développer un marché financier plus profond, dynamique et attractif, capable d'accompagner les entreprises, les infrastructures et les grands projets de transformation économique du Cameroun et de la CEMAC. Pour le Minfi, l'enjeu est clair : canaliser l'épargne longue vers les secteurs productifs, renforcer la confiance des investisseurs et améliorer les mécanismes de financement des PME, trop souvent exclues du circuit bancaire classique. Cette première édition, qui se veut une plateforme de réflexion et de mise en relation entre investisseurs, émetteurs, régulateurs et entrepreneurs, intervient dans un contexte de besoin accru en financements pour l'industrialisation et les infrastructures. Le Ministre a ainsi appelé à accélérer les réformes, à innover dans les instruments financiers et à renforcer l'éducation financière pour bâtir un marché des capitaux au service de la croissance inclusive. Cet article Diamond Capital Convention 2026 : le MINFI appelle à orienter les capitaux vers l'économie réelle est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .
